2027-03-07.title: K'piphtho Sunday · The Healing of the Bent Woman
readings: I give you thanks, O Lord and King
The Lord has opened my ear
2027-03-07.alt: Fifth Sunday of the Great Fast.
2027-03-07.verse: Woman, you are set free from your ailment.
theo: In a synagogue on the sabbath there is a woman who “had a spirit that had crippled her for eighteen years. She was bent over and was quite unable to stand up straight.” For eighteen years she has looked only at the ground. Jesus sees her, calls her, and says: “Woman, you are set free from your ailment.” He lays his hands on her, “and immediately she stood up straight and began praising God.”

The leader of the synagogue is indignant: healing is work, and work is forbidden on the sabbath. Jesus answers: you untie your ox and donkey on the sabbath to give them water; “ought not this woman, a daughter of Abraham whom Satan bound for eighteen long years, be set free from this bondage on the sabbath day?” The sabbath is the day of God's rest, and God's rest is our freedom.

Many of us are bent: by guilt, by worry, by addiction, by years of carrying burdens alone, by sins we have stopped noticing. We get used to looking at the ground. The Fast is the time when Jesus calls us, lays his hands on us, and lets us stand straight again and look up to God.

The evening Gospel, the Good Samaritan, shows us how to be Christ's hands for others: “moved with pity”, he bound up the wounded man's wounds. St Paul says: “present your bodies as a living sacrifice… Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your minds… Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep.” Healed ourselves, we become healers: “Go and do likewise.”
conn: A daughter of Abraham.
Jesus restores her dignity: not just a patient, but a daughter of the covenant, like Zacchaeus, “a son of Abraham” (Luke 19:9).
The Good Samaritan.
The Fathers saw Christ himself in the Samaritan: he came down to wounded humanity, poured oil and wine, and brought us to the inn of the Church.
The opened ear.
Isaiah 50:4–5: “Morning by morning he wakens my ear”; the servant of the Lord listens and does not turn back.
Blessing for evil.
1 Peter 3:9: “Do not repay evil for evil… but, on the contrary, repay with a blessing.”
altar: At every Holy Qurbono the Good Samaritan pours the oil and wine of his grace into our wounds. We leave the altar standing straighter, called to bend down to the wounded on our road.
outline: Opening
Eighteen years looking at the ground: what bends us?
Point 1 · Jesus sees and calls
He notices the one no one notices.
Point 2 · Set free on the sabbath
God's rest is our freedom; Sunday as a day of healing.
Point 3 · Stand up and praise
Healing leads to worship.
Point 4 · Go and do likewise
The Good Samaritan: be Christ's hands for the wounded.
Take-home line
“You are set free.”
live: Name what bends you
Bring one burden or habit to Jesus in Confession or prayer this week.
Be a Samaritan (Luke 10:37)
Stop for one person in need you would usually pass by.
Make Sunday a day of rest and healing
Keep Sunday for God, family and works of mercy.
fathers: St Augustine
The Samaritan is our Lord, who became our neighbour; he bound our wounds, set us on his own beast, and brought us to the inn, the Church, until he returns (Sermon 171; On Christian Doctrine I).
St Ambrose of Milan
The bent woman is an image of the soul bowed down to earthly things; Christ's hand raises it to look to heaven (Exposition of the Gospel of Luke 7).
magis: Catechism 2172–2173
The sabbath is a day of freedom from work and for the works of mercy; Jesus healed on the sabbath to show this.
Catechism 1825, 2447
Love of neighbour and the works of mercy, spiritual and corporal.
Fratelli Tutti 56–86
Pope Francis on the Good Samaritan: we are all called to stop and bend down to the wounded.
saints: 9 Mar: the Forty Martyrs of Sebaste. 14 Mar: Samio Sunday.
2027-03-07.prayer: Lord Jesus, you saw the bent woman, called her, and set her free. Lay your hands on us in this Fast: lift what bends us down, let us stand straight and praise you, and make us Good Samaritans for the wounded on our road. Amen.

2027-03-14.title: Samio Sunday · The Healing of the Blind
readings: Solomon asks for an understanding mind
The Lord made the earth by his power
2027-03-14.alt: Sixth Sunday of the Great Fast. The Fortieth Day of the Fast is Friday 19 March; Lazarus Saturday is 20 March; Hosanna Sunday is 21 March: remind the faithful to bring palm leaves and flowers.
2027-03-14.verse: One thing I do know, that though I was blind, now I see.
theo: On the last Sunday before Holy Week the Church reads two healings of the blind. In John, Jesus meets a man blind from birth. The disciples ask whose sin caused it. Jesus answers: “Neither this man nor his parents sinned; he was born blind so that God's works might be revealed in him… As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world.” He makes mud, anoints the man's eyes, and sends him: “Go, wash in the pool of Siloam (which means Sent).”

The healed man is questioned again and again by the Pharisees. He does not know all the theology, but he knows one thing: “Though I was blind, now I see.” Step by step his sight grows: first “the man called Jesus”, then “a prophet”, then, kneeling before him, “Lord, I believe.” Meanwhile those who claim to see become blind. Jesus says: “I came into this world for judgment so that those who do not see may see, and those who do see may become blind.”

In Mark, blind Bartimaeus sits by the road at Jericho and cries out: “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!” People tell him to be quiet; he cries out louder. Jesus asks: “What do you want me to do for you?” “My teacher, let me see again.” “Go; your faith has made you well.” And Bartimaeus “followed him on the way”, the way to Jerusalem and the Cross.

Job, after all his suffering, says: “I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you.” This is the goal of the Fast: not only to hear about God, but to see him with the eyes of faith. In Baptism, called “enlightenment” by the Fathers, we were washed and given sight. As Holy Week begins, let us ask with Bartimaeus: “Lord, let me see,” and then follow Jesus on the way.
conn: Siloam, “Sent”.
The man washes in the pool called Sent, and Jesus is the One sent by the Father: the Fathers saw here an image of Baptism, the washing that gives sight.
Clay and anointing.
Jesus makes clay as God formed Adam from the earth (Genesis 2:7): a new creation.
Solomon's prayer.
Solomon asked for an understanding mind (1 Kings 3:9); true sight is wisdom from God.
Following on the way.
Bartimaeus follows Jesus “on the way” to Jerusalem (Mark 10:52): healed disciples walk with him to the Cross.
altar: The Fathers called Baptism “illumination” and the Eucharist the food of those who see. At the Holy Qurbono we pray with Bartimaeus: “Have mercy on us”, and we receive the Light of the world.
outline: Opening
What is the worst kind of blindness?
Point 1 · Light of the world
Jesus opens eyes: new creation, Siloam, Baptism.
Point 2 · Growing sight
From “a man called Jesus” to “Lord, I believe”.
Point 3 · Those who think they see
Pride blinds: the Pharisees.
Point 4 · Follow on the way
Bartimaeus: cry out, receive sight, follow to Jerusalem.
Take-home line
“Lord, let me see.”
live: Pray Bartimaeus' prayer
Repeat during the day: “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me.”
Prepare for Holy Week
Bring palm leaves and flowers on Sunday; plan to attend the services of Holy Week.
Honest measures (Deuteronomy 25:13)
Examine honesty in business, weights, wages and taxes.
fathers: St Augustine
The man born blind is the human race; the clay is the Word made flesh; the washing in Siloam is Baptism, by which we are enlightened (Tractates on John 44).
St Ephrem the Syrian
With the clay he formed eyes as he had formed Adam from the dust; the Creator showed himself in the creating hand (Commentary on the Diatessaron).
magis: Catechism 1216
Baptism is called “enlightenment”, because those who receive it are enlightened in their understanding.
Catechism 2616
Jesus hears the prayer of faith: “Son of David, have mercy on me”; the Jesus Prayer comes from such cries.
Lumen Fidei 1–4
Faith is a light that illumines every aspect of human existence.
saints: 17 Mar: St Patrick. 18 Mar: St Cyril of Jerusalem. 19 Mar: St Joseph, and in 2027 also the Fortieth Day of the Great Fast. 20 Mar: Lazarus Saturday.
2027-03-14.prayer: Lord Jesus, light of the world, you opened the eyes of the man born blind and of Bartimaeus. Have mercy on us: heal our blindness, let us see you with the eyes of faith, and give us grace to follow you on the way to Jerusalem, to your Cross and your Resurrection. Amen.

2027-03-21.title: Hosanna Sunday · The Lord's Entry into Jerusalem
readings: If these were silent, the stones would shout
The scepter shall not depart from Judah
The ark is brought to Jerusalem
Your king comes, humble, riding on a donkey
A great multitude with palm branches
Hosanna! Blessed is the one who comes
2027-03-21.alt: Hosanna (Palm) Sunday. Holy Week (Hasho) begins this evening: special prayers and abstinence. In the 2025–26 lectionary this Sunday was also Social Welfare Day.
2027-03-21.verse: Hosanna! Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord—the King of Israel!
theo: Today Jesus enters Jerusalem, and the crowds go out to meet him with palm branches, shouting: “Hosanna! Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord—the King of Israel!” Zechariah had foretold it: “Lo, your king comes to you; triumphant and victorious is he, humble and riding on a donkey.” He comes as King, but not as the kings of this world: not on a war horse, but on a donkey, the animal of peace.

The Pharisees tell Jesus to silence his disciples. He answers: “I tell you, if these were silent, the stones would shout out.” All creation recognises its King. In our Malankara churches the palms are blessed and carried in procession, and we join the crowd of Jerusalem, and, as Revelation shows, the great multitude in heaven “robed in white, with palm branches in their hands”, crying: “Salvation belongs to our God… and to the Lamb!”

But we know where this road leads. The same city that shouts “Hosanna” will soon shout “Crucify him”. The King enters Jerusalem to be enthroned on the Cross. Genesis promised that “the scepter shall not depart from Judah”; the King from Judah reigns from the wood of the Cross. The ark of the covenant was brought into Jerusalem with joy and fear (2 Samuel 6); now the true Ark, God dwelling among us, enters the city.

Hosanna means “Save us, we pray.” It is a cry of praise and a cry for help. As Holy Week begins this evening, let us carry our palms home not as decorations but as a promise: Lord, I welcome you as my King; save me; and give me grace to follow you this week, through the Cross to the Resurrection.
conn: The humble king.
Zechariah 9:9 is fulfilled to the letter (John 12:15); his kingdom brings peace “from sea to sea” (Zechariah 9:10).
Palms in heaven.
Revelation 7:9: the palms of Jerusalem become the palms of the martyrs and saints before the Lamb.
The Lion of Judah.
Genesis 49:9–10: Judah the lion's whelp; the scepter shall not depart; Revelation 5:5 names Christ “the Lion of the tribe of Judah”.
Grafted in.
Romans 11:17: we Gentiles have been grafted into the olive tree of Israel; we too shout Hosanna to Israel's King.
altar: Every Holy Qurbono repeats the cry of Palm Sunday: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, Hosanna in the highest.” The One who entered Jerusalem enters our altar and our hearts.
outline: Opening
The procession: why palms?
Point 1 · The humble King
On a donkey, not a war horse: a kingdom of peace.
Point 2 · Stones would shout
All creation recognises Christ; our praise must not fall silent.
Point 3 · From Hosanna to Crucify
The fickleness of the crowd, and of our hearts.
Point 4 · Hosanna: save us
Enter Holy Week with Christ.
Take-home line
“Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes.”
live: Keep Holy Week
Take part in the services of Pesaha, Good Friday, Holy Saturday and the Resurrection.
Keep your palm
Place the blessed palm by the cross at home and pray there each evening this week.
Make peace
Be reconciled with someone before Easter, as the King of peace enters your home.
fathers: St Andrew of Crete
“Let us run to accompany him as he hastens towards his passion… Let us spread before his feet not garments or branches, but ourselves” (Sermon 9 on Palm Sunday).
St Augustine

The Lord was King of Israel not to exact tribute or command armies, but to rule souls and bring them to the kingdom of heaven; it was no gain to the King of the ages to become King of men, but a sign of his mercy (Tractates on John 51).
magis: Catechism 559–560
Jesus enters Jerusalem as the Messiah, the Son of David, on a donkey; the Church's liturgy opens Holy Week with this feast.
Catechism 1352
The Sanctus with its Hosanna joins the Church's praise to the angels' song.
Catechism 571
The Paschal mystery of Christ's Cross and Resurrection stands at the centre of the Good News.
saints: Monday 22 to Wednesday 24 March: days of Holy Week. Thursday 25 March: Pesaha (Maundy Thursday); in 2027 this is also the date of the Annunciation, so check how your eparchy keeps it. Friday 26 March: Good Friday. Saturday 27 March: Holy Saturday. Sunday 28 March: Qyomtho, the Resurrection.
2027-03-21.prayer: Lord Jesus, humble King, you entered Jerusalem on a donkey to give your life for us. Hosanna: save us! As we carry our palms, give us faithful hearts that do not change from praise to rejection, and lead us through your Passion to the joy of your Resurrection. Amen.

2027-03-25.title: Pesaha · The Lord's Supper
readings: Let anyone who is thirsty come to me
Do not walk with those who lie in wait for blood
The Lord will reign on Mount Zion
The marriage supper of the Lamb
Do this in remembrance of me
2027-03-25.alt: Pesaha (Maundy Thursday). In 2027 the date of the Annunciation (25 March) falls on this day; follow the direction of your eparchy on how the Annunciation is kept.
2027-03-25.verse: Then he took a loaf of bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it and gave it to them, saying, “This is my body, which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of me.”
theo: On the night before he suffered, Jesus gathered his apostles in the upper room. “I have eagerly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer.” At that table he took bread, gave thanks, broke it and said: “This is my body, which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of me.” And after supper he took the cup: “This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood.” On this night the Holy Qurbono was born.

Exodus tells of the first Passover: a lamb without blemish, its blood on the doorposts, eaten in haste by a people ready to leave slavery. “When I see the blood, I will pass over you.” Jesus is the true Passover Lamb. His blood marks us, his Body feeds us for the journey from slavery to freedom, from death to life.

At the same table Jesus gave his apostles a lesson in greatness: “Who is greater, the one who is at the table or the one who serves? Is it not the one at the table? But I am among you as one who serves.” In our tradition the washing of feet makes this visible. The Eucharist and service cannot be separated: the One who gives his Body washes our feet.

St Paul hands on what he received: “For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord's death until he comes.” He also warns against receiving unworthily. Pesaha is the night to thank God for the Holy Qurbono and the priesthood, to examine our hearts, and to stay awake with Jesus as he goes out to Gethsemane.
conn: The Passover lamb.
Exodus 12: the unblemished lamb whose blood saves; John 1:29 and 1 Corinthians 5:7: “Christ, our paschal lamb, has been sacrificed.”
The Day of Atonement.
Leviticus 16: the high priest enters the Holy of Holies with blood; Christ is priest and victim (Hebrews 9:11–14).
Rivers of living water.
John 7:37–38: from the heart of Christ flow streams of living water, fulfilled when his side is pierced (John 19:34).
The wedding supper of the Lamb.
Revelation 19:9: “Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb”: every Qurbono is a foretaste.
altar: Tonight we celebrate the Holy Qurbono at the very hour of its institution. The words the priest says over the bread and wine are the words of the upper room. Thank God tonight for every Qurbono you have received, and for the priests who celebrate it.
outline: Opening
The upper room: “I have eagerly desired to eat this Passover with you.”
Point 1 · The true Passover
From the lamb of Egypt to the Lamb of God.
Point 2 · “This is my body”
The real presence: Christ gives himself.
Point 3 · The one who serves
The washing of feet: Eucharist and service.
Point 4 · Stay with him
Gethsemane: watch and pray with Jesus tonight.
Take-home line
“Do this in remembrance of me.”
live: Pesaha at home
Share the Pesaha appam and paal as a family, praying for unity and remembering the Last Supper.
Watch one hour
Spend time in adoration tonight, keeping Jesus company.
Serve someone
Do one humble service for a family member this week, as Jesus washed feet.
fathers: St Cyril of Jerusalem

“Since he himself has declared and said of the bread, This is my Body, who shall dare to doubt any longer? … Do not regard the bread and wine as simple elements, for they are, according to the Lord’s declaration, the Body and Blood of Christ” (Mystagogical Catecheses 4, 1 and 6).
St John Chrysostom

“It is not man who makes the gifts become the Body and Blood of Christ, but Christ himself, who was crucified for us. The priest stands there carrying out the action, but the power and grace are of God” (Homily on the Betrayal of Judas 1, 6).
magis: Catechism 1337–1340
The Lord instituted the Eucharist at the Last Supper as the memorial of his death and Resurrection, the new Passover.
Ecclesia de Eucharistia 3–5
The Church draws her life from the Eucharist; it was born in the upper room.
Catechism 1366–1367
The Eucharist is a sacrifice because it re-presents the sacrifice of the Cross.
saints: Friday 26 March: Good Friday (the collection is for the Holy Land). Saturday 27 March: Holy Saturday. Sunday 28 March: Qyomtho, the Resurrection.
2027-03-25.prayer: Lord Jesus, on the night you were betrayed you gave us your Body and Blood and washed your disciples' feet. Thank you for the Holy Qurbono and for the priesthood. Make us worthy to receive you, humble to serve one another, and faithful to stay with you in your agony. Amen.

2027-03-26.title: Good Friday · The Passion and Death of our Lord
readings: Readings of the Hours of Good Friday
Not listed in the Sacred Lectionary; follow the Hasho (Holy Week) book
The Gospels of the Passion read through the day
2027-03-26.alt: Good Friday. A day of fasting. The collection of the day is for the Holy Land, as directed by the Holy Father.
2027-03-26.verse: When Jesus had received the wine, he said, “It is finished.” Then he bowed his head and gave up his spirit.
theo: On Good Friday the Church stands at the foot of the Cross. The One who entered Jerusalem to the cry of Hosanna is condemned, mocked, scourged, crowned with thorns, and crucified outside the city between two criminals. The Holy One is counted among the wicked. The prophet had seen it long before: “He was wounded for our transgressions, crushed for our iniquities… and by his bruises we are healed” (Isaiah 53:5).

From the Cross Jesus speaks words that the Church treasures. “Father, forgive them; for they do not know what they are doing.” To the repentant thief: “Truly I tell you, today you will be with me in Paradise.” To his Mother and the beloved disciple: “Woman, here is your son… Here is your mother.” Then the cry of the abandoned: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” And at the end: “It is finished”, and “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit.”

“It is finished” is not a cry of defeat but of completion. The work the Father gave him is accomplished: the true Lamb has been sacrificed, the new covenant sealed in his blood. A soldier pierces his side, “and at once blood and water came out” (John 19:34). The Fathers saw in that blood and water the Eucharist and Baptism, the Church born from the side of Christ as Eve from the side of Adam.

On this day there is no Holy Qurbono in our tradition; the altar is bare because the Lamb himself is offered on the Cross. We venerate the Cross, we keep fast and silence, and we stand with Mary, who did not run away. The wood of shame has become the tree of life. “We adore you, O Christ, and we bless you, because by your holy Cross you have redeemed the world.”
conn: The Suffering Servant.
Isaiah 52:13–53:12 describes the Passion centuries before it happened.
The tree of life.
The tree in Eden brought death; the tree of the Cross brings life (Genesis 2:9; Revelation 22:2).
The bronze serpent.
“As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up” (John 3:14; Numbers 21:9).
The new Adam's side.
As Eve was formed from Adam's side, the Church is born from the pierced side of Christ (John 19:34).
altar: Today the altar stands bare and there is no Holy Qurbono, for the one Sacrifice is contemplated on the Cross. Every Qurbono we celebrate makes present this same sacrifice of Calvary; today we simply kneel before it.
outline: Opening
Silence before the Cross.
Point 1 · Wounded for us
Isaiah 53: by his bruises we are healed.
Point 2 · The words from the Cross
Forgiveness, Paradise, Mary, abandonment, completion, surrender.
Point 3 · Blood and water
The Church and the sacraments born from his side.
Point 4 · Stand with Mary
Do not run away; venerate the Cross.
Take-home line
“By your holy Cross you have redeemed the world.”
live: Keep the fast
Fast today with love, offering it for those who suffer.
Forgive (Luke 23:34)
Forgive one person today, as Jesus forgave from the Cross.
Venerate the Cross
Take part in the Good Friday service and kiss the Cross with gratitude.
fathers: St John Chrysostom
“There flowed from his side water and blood… the symbols of Baptism and the Mysteries. From these two the Church is born… as Eve was formed from the side of Adam” (Catechesis 3, 13–19).
St Cyril of Jerusalem
“He stretched out his hands on the Cross, that he might embrace the ends of the world; for Golgotha is the centre of the earth” (Catechetical Lectures 13, 28).
magis: Catechism 613–618
Christ's death is the Paschal sacrifice that accomplishes the definitive redemption of humanity; he offered himself freely.
Catechism 964
Mary's union with her Son in the work of salvation is shown at the foot of the Cross.
Catechism 766
The Church is born primarily of Christ's total self-giving: from the side of Christ asleep on the Cross.
saints: Saturday 27 March: Holy Saturday. Sunday 28 March: Qyomtho, the Resurrection.
2027-03-26.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, crucified for us, we adore you and we bless you, because by your holy Cross you have redeemed the world. Forgive us, remember us in your kingdom, give us your Mother as our mother, and let us die with you to sin, that we may rise with you to life. Amen.

2027-03-27.title: Holy Saturday · The Lord Rests in the Tomb
readings: Hush! We must not mention the name of the Lord
Buried with him by baptism into death
The tomb is sealed and guarded
2027-03-27.alt: Holy Saturday. The Church waits at the tomb. In the night the celebration of the Resurrection begins.
2027-03-27.verse: So they went with the guard and made the tomb secure by sealing the stone.
theo: Holy Saturday is the day of great silence. The body of the Lord lies in the tomb of Joseph of Arimathea. The disciples are hidden in fear; the women wait for the sabbath to pass. His enemies, remembering his words about rising on the third day, ask Pilate for a guard; “so they went with the guard and made the tomb secure by sealing the stone.” They seal the tomb, not knowing that they are preparing witnesses to the Resurrection.

The Creed says: “he descended to the dead.” While his body rested in the tomb, Christ went down to the realm of the dead to bring the good news to the just who had waited for him, from Adam onwards. The Eastern Churches love the image of Christ breaking the gates of Sheol and taking Adam and Eve by the hand. Holy Saturday is not empty: it is the hidden victory.

St Paul explains what this means for us: “we have been buried with him by baptism into death, so that, just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life.” Our Baptism was a burial and a resurrection. Today we let die in us whatever must die, so that tonight we may rise with him.
Mary, his Mother, kept faith on this day when everyone else despaired. Let us keep this day in quiet prayer, with her, waiting in hope for the light of Qyomtho.
conn: The sign of Jonah.
“As Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the sea monster, so for three days and three nights the Son of Man will be in the heart of the earth” (Matthew 12:40).
The sabbath rest.
God rested on the seventh day after creation (Genesis 2:2); Christ rests in the tomb on the sabbath after the work of the new creation.
Buried with him.
Romans 6:4: Baptism is our burial and resurrection with Christ.
The sealed stone.
The guards and the seal, meant to prevent a resurrection, become witnesses of it (Matthew 28:4, 11).
altar: The altar waits in silence; tonight it will be the place of the risen Lord. Like Mary, we keep watch, so that when the Qurbono of the Resurrection is celebrated our hearts are ready.
outline: Opening
The silence of Holy Saturday.
Point 1 · The sealed tomb
Human power tries to keep God in the grave.
Point 2 · He descended to the dead
Christ brings light to Adam and the just of old.
Point 3 · Buried with him
Baptism: let the old self die.
Point 4 · Waiting with Mary
Hope when all seems lost.
Take-home line
“If we have died with him, we shall live with him.”
live: Keep silence
Spend part of today in quiet prayer, without television or phone.
Prepare for the night
Make your Easter Confession if you have not yet; prepare your home for the feast.
Pray with Mary
Pray the Sorrowful Mysteries or the Stabat Mater with her.
fathers: An ancient homily for Holy Saturday

“Something strange is happening: there is a great silence on earth… because the King is asleep. God has died in the flesh and has gone to rouse those who have slept ever since the world began… He took Adam by the hand: Awake, O sleeper” (ancient homily, read in the Liturgy of the Hours).
St Ephrem the Syrian
Death received him and was itself undone; Sheol could not hold him, and the dead heard his voice (Nisibene Hymns).
magis: Catechism 631–635
Jesus descended into the realm of the dead as Saviour, proclaiming the Good News to the spirits imprisoned there; this is the last phase of his messianic mission.
Catechism 624–630
Christ's burial: the mystery of Holy Saturday, when Christ lying in the tomb reveals God's great sabbath rest.
Catechism 1214–1215
Baptism signifies and actually brings about death to sin and entry into the life of the Trinity.
saints: Sunday 28 March: Qyomtho, the Resurrection of our Lord; Holy Qurbono for the people.
2027-03-27.prayer: Lord Jesus, you rested in the tomb and went down to those who sat in darkness. Bury with you all that is dead in us, keep us in hope with your Mother, and raise us with you to newness of life. Amen.

2027-03-28.title: Qyomtho · The Resurrection of our Lord
readings: He is not here; he has been raised
Daniel brought up from the lions' den
Peace, peace, to the far and the near
God raised this Jesus; we are witnesses
Christ died, was buried, and was raised
2027-03-28.alt: Qyomtho, Easter. Holy Qurbono for the people. The season of Qyomtho begins; this week is Hevoro (white) week.
2027-03-28.verse: He is not here; for he has been raised, as he said.
theo: Christ is risen! Very early on the first day of the week, the women go to the tomb, and an angel says: “Do not be afraid; I know that you are looking for Jesus who was crucified. He is not here; for he has been raised, as he said.” Then Jesus himself meets them: “Greetings!” They take hold of his feet and worship him. The One who was dead is alive for ever.

In John's Gospel Mary Magdalene runs to Peter and the beloved disciple; they run to the tomb and find the linen cloths lying there. The other disciple “saw and believed”. The empty tomb is not proof by itself, but it is the first sign; faith is born when we see with the heart that God has kept his word.

The Old Testament readings have prepared us. Daniel is brought up alive from the lions' den, because God shut the lions' mouths (Daniel 6:22). Moses sets up the tabernacle, and God's glory fills it. Isaiah announces: “Peace, peace, to the far and the near.” In the risen Christ the glory of God dwells among us for ever, and his first word to the disciples will be: “Peace be with you.”

St Peter preaches on the day of Pentecost: “This Jesus God raised up, and of that all of us are witnesses.” St Paul hands on the heart of the Gospel: “Christ died for our sins in accordance with the scriptures… he was buried… he was raised on the third day.” Easter is not a beautiful story; it is the event on which everything stands. Because Christ is risen, sin is forgiven, death is defeated, and our own bodies will rise. Let us live as Easter people.
conn: Daniel and the lions.
Daniel, sealed in the den with a stone (Daniel 6:17), comes out alive at dawn: a figure of the sealed tomb and the risen Lord.
The tabernacle.
Exodus 40: God's dwelling is set up on the first day of the first month; the risen body of Christ is the true temple (John 2:19–21).
Peace to the far and the near.
Isaiah 57:19 and Ephesians 2:17: the risen Christ preaches peace to all.
The third day.
Hosea 6:2 and Jonah 1:17: the third day of God's saving action.
altar: Every Sunday is a little Easter, and every Holy Qurbono is the meeting with the risen Lord. As the women held his feet, we receive his risen Body. Today let us receive him with Easter joy.
outline: Opening
Christ is risen! He is risen indeed!
Point 1 · The empty tomb
“He is not here; he has been raised, as he said.” God keeps his word.
Point 2 · Meeting the risen Lord
The women, Mary Magdalene, Peter and John: faith is born.
Point 3 · Witnesses
Peter: “we are witnesses”; we too are sent.
Point 4 · Easter people
Sin forgiven, death defeated, hope for the body; live it this week.
Take-home line
“He is not here; he is risen!”
live: Greet with Easter joy
Greet family and friends with “Christ is risen!” throughout Easter week.
Visit someone sad
Bring Easter joy to a sick, elderly or grieving person.
Keep the Sundays
Resolve to keep every Sunday as a little Easter: Qurbono, rest, family.
fathers: St John Chrysostom

“Let no one fear death, for the Saviour's death has set us free… Christ is risen, and the demons are fallen; Christ is risen, and the angels rejoice; Christ is risen, and life reigns” (Paschal Homily).
St Ephrem the Syrian
“Glory to you, who put on our body and went down to Sheol, and rose and raised us with you” (Nisibene Hymns).
magis: Catechism 638–658
The Resurrection of Christ is the crowning truth of our faith; it is a real, historical event with a transcendent character, confirming all that Christ taught.
Catechism 1169
Easter is the “feast of feasts”, the “solemnity of solemnities”.
Catechism 989–990
We firmly believe that, as Christ is truly risen, the righteous will live for ever with him and he will raise them up on the last day.
saints: The week after Qyomtho is kept with joy. Next Sunday: New Sunday (the appearance to Thomas).
2027-03-28.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, you have trampled down death by death and given life to those in the tombs. Fill us with Easter joy and peace, make us witnesses of your Resurrection, and raise us with you on the last day. Christ is risen! He is truly risen! Amen.

2027-03-01.title: Monday of the fourth week of the Great Fast
readings: Abraham prays, and God heals Abimelech's house
May the Lord of peace give you peace at all times
Jesus walks on the sea; Peter cries, “Lord, save me!”
2027-03-01.alt: Great Fast (Valiya Nombu), fourth week. The Great Fast passes its middle this week; Mid-Lent is kept on Wednesday.
2027-03-01.verse: Take heart, it is I; do not be afraid.
theo: The first reading finishes the story of Abraham in Gerar. Abimelech, warned by God in a dream, rises early and confronts Abraham: “What have you done to us? How have I sinned against you, that you have brought such great guilt on me and my kingdom?” Abraham's answer is honest about his fear: “I did it because I thought, There is no fear of God at all in this place, and they will kill me because of my wife.” He had judged a whole people without knowing them, and he was wrong: the pagan king turned out to fear God more than Abraham expected. Abimelech returns Sarah, gives gifts, and opens his land: “My land is before you; settle where it pleases you.” Then comes the turning point: “Abraham prayed to God; and God healed Abimelech, and also healed his wife and female slaves.” The man who caused the harm becomes the one who prays for healing. Here is a Lenten pattern: we acknowledge the wrong we have done, and then we pray, sincerely, for the very people we have wronged.

In the Gospel, fear meets Jesus on the water. The disciples are battling the wind through the night, and when they see Jesus walking toward them on the sea they cry out, “It is a ghost!” He answers at once: “Take heart, it is I; do not be afraid.” Peter steps out, walks, and then looks at the wind instead of the Lord: “beginning to sink, he cried out, ‘Lord, save me!’ Jesus immediately reached out his hand and caught him.” St Augustine said that Peter sank because he trusted in himself, and rose because he cried out to the Lord; in himself he was weak, in Christ he was strong (in substance). Halfway through the Fast, many of us feel the wind more than at the beginning. The prayer of Peter is short enough for any moment: Lord, save me. And Paul's blessing is the answer to it: “Now may the Lord of peace himself give you peace at all times in all ways. The Lord be with all of you.”
outline: Opening
Ask: when did fear make you misjudge a person or a situation?
Point 1 · Abraham prays for Abimelech
The one who caused harm prays for healing.
Point 2 · Take heart, it is I
Jesus comes to us in the storm.
Point 3 · Lord, save me
The hand that catches Peter; the Lord of peace.
Take-home line
“Take heart, it is I; do not be afraid.”
live: Pray for the one you wronged (Genesis 20:17)
Think of one person you have hurt or misjudged, and pray for him or her by name every day this week.
Say Peter's prayer (Matthew 14:30)
Each time fear or temptation rises today, say slowly: Lord, save me.
2027-03-01.prayer: Lord Jesus, you came to your disciples walking on the sea, and you said to them: take heart, it is I; do not be afraid. When we judge others out of fear, correct us; when we have hurt others, teach us to pray for them as Abraham prayed for Abimelech. When the wind is strong and we begin to sink, stretch out your hand and catch us. Lord of peace, give us your peace at all times and in all ways, in this Great Fast and always. Amen.
altar: In the Holy Qurbono the same Lord who said “it is I” comes to us, truly present, and the priest's blessing “peace be with you all” echoes Paul's prayer for the Lord of peace.

2027-03-02.title: Tuesday of the fourth week of the Great Fast
readings: The birth of Isaac: God has brought laughter
Clothed with Christ, heirs according to the promise
Woe to the cities that did not repent
2027-03-02.verse: God has brought laughter for me; everyone who hears will laugh with me.
theo: After twenty-five years of waiting, the promise is kept. “The Lord dealt with Sarah as he had said, and the Lord did for Sarah as he had promised. Sarah conceived and bore Abraham a son in his old age, at the time of which God had spoken to him.” Notice how often the reading repeats it: as he had said, as he had promised, as God had spoken. Abraham names the boy Isaac, which means “he laughs.” Years before, Sarah had laughed in disbelief behind the tent door; now she laughs for joy: “God has brought laughter for me; everyone who hears will laugh with me.” The same woman, the same laughter, but turned inside out by the faithfulness of God. Early Fathers such as St Ambrose saw in Isaac, the son of promise born when nature had given up hope, a figure of Christ, the true joy of the world (in substance). The Great Fast is not a season of gloom; it prepares us for the laughter of Easter, when God keeps his greatest promise.

Paul tells us whose children we are: “for in Christ Jesus you are all children of God through faith. As many of you as were baptized into Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ.” In our baptism we were clothed in a white garment; in Christ there is “no longer Jew or Greek, there is no longer slave or free, there is no longer male and female; for all of you are one in Christ Jesus. And if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to the promise.” The laughter of Sarah has become the inheritance of every baptized person. But an inheritance can be neglected. In the Gospel Jesus reproaches the towns around the lake, Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum, which had seen most of his miracles and still did not change: “if the deeds of power done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes.” We who have received the sacraments, the Word and the Holy Qurbono every week have seen more than Tyre and Sidon ever saw. The Fast asks whether all that grace has changed us.
outline: Opening
Ask: what promise of God are you still waiting for?
Point 1 · As he had promised
Isaac is born; Sarah's laughter of joy.
Point 2 · Clothed with Christ
Children of God, heirs of the promise.
Point 3 · Woe to Chorazin
Much grace, and no change.
Take-home line
“God has brought laughter for me.”
live: Remember your baptism (Galatians 3:27)
Find out the date of your baptism and thank God for it today; if you have your baptismal candle or photo, bring it to the family prayer corner.
Let grace change you (Matthew 11:21)
Name one grace you have received again and again, and one change it should produce in you; make that change this week.
2027-03-02.prayer: Faithful God, you did for Sarah as you had promised, and you turned her laughter of doubt into laughter of joy. You have clothed us with Christ in baptism and made us heirs of your promise. Do not let the many graces we receive pass over us without fruit. Give us repentant hearts in this Great Fast, and bring us at last to the joy of the Resurrection. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.
altar: Each Holy Qurbono is a deed of power done in our midst: Christ himself, truly present, given to children of God who were clothed with him in baptism.

2027-03-03.title: Mid-Lent · Wednesday of the fourth week of the Great Fast · The Exaltation of the Cross in the middle of the Fast
readings: The Son of Man will be betrayed, killed, and raised
The bronze serpent lifted on a pole
Samuel prays at Mizpah; the people fast
O taste and see that the Lord is good
They shall look on the one whom they have pierced
No burden beyond what is necessary
The rock was Christ; God is faithful
As Moses lifted up the serpent, so must the Son of Man be lifted up
2027-03-03.alt: Great Fast (Valiya Nombu), fourth week. Mid-Lent (Pakuthi Nombu): the Panchangam names the day “the setting up of Golgotha.” At the middle of the Great Fast the Church lifts up the Holy Cross. In many parishes the Cross is set up in the middle of the church, honoured with a procession and hymns, and kept there for veneration through the rest of the Fast. Customs vary; follow your parish.
2027-03-03.verse: And just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that whoever believes in him may have eternal life.
theo: Today we stand at the middle of the Great Fast, and our Church does something striking: it lifts up the Cross. The Panchangam calls this day Pakuthi Nombu, Mid-Lent, and names it “the setting up of Golgotha.” In the Syriac tradition the faithful who have been walking through the Fast are shown, halfway, where the road leads: to the hill of Calvary, where the Cross will stand, and to the empty tomb beyond it. The Cross set up in the middle of the church is like a milestone and a signpost together. It tells weary travellers: you are not lost; this is where we are going; and this is what will give you strength for the rest of the way. Many of us have begun to tire. Some resolutions have already slipped. The Church does not scold; she lifts up the Cross and says: look.

The readings explain why looking is enough. In the wilderness the people grew “impatient on the way” and spoke against God and Moses, and poisonous serpents bit them. When they confessed, “We have sinned,” God did not simply remove the serpents. He told Moses: “Make a poisonous serpent, and set it on a pole; and everyone who is bitten shall look at it and live.” Jesus himself takes up this image in the Gospel: “And just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that whoever believes in him may have eternal life. For God so loved the world that he gave his only Son, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but may have eternal life.” St John Chrysostom explained that in the wilderness the bronze image of a serpent healed bodies from the bite of real serpents, while on the Cross Christ, in the likeness of sinful flesh yet without sin, heals souls from the bite of the ancient serpent (in substance). The cure looks like the wound: the Son of God takes our curse upon himself so that we, looking at him in faith, may live.

The other readings fill out the picture. Zechariah foresees a day when God will “pour out a spirit of compassion and supplication” and the people “look on the one whom they have pierced” and mourn for him “as one mourns for an only child.” St John saw this fulfilled at Calvary. Samuel gathers Israel at Mizpah, where they fast, pour out water before the Lord, and confess, “We have sinned against the Lord,” and Samuel cries out to God for them; later he will set up a stone there and say, “Thus far the Lord has helped us.” That is a perfect Mid-Lent prayer. Paul reminds the Corinthians that their ancestors in the desert “drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ,” warns them not to put Christ to the test “as some of them did, and were destroyed by serpents,” and then encourages them: “God is faithful, and he will not let you be tested beyond your strength, but with the testing he will also provide the way out so that you may be able to endure it.” The apostles in Acts lift needless burdens from the Gentile believers, and the evening Gospel already announces the Passion and the third day. And the Psalm gives the response of the whole day: “Look to him, and be radiant; so your faces shall never be ashamed… O taste and see that the Lord is good.” We look at the Cross, and we taste the Lord's goodness in the Holy Qurbono, where the One lifted up on Golgotha gives us his Body and Blood.
conn: The bronze serpent and the Cross.
Numbers 21 and John 3:14–15: the sign lifted up in the desert points to the Son of Man lifted up on the Cross; looking in faith brings life.
The pierced one.
Zechariah 12:10 is quoted in John 19:37 at the piercing of Jesus' side: “They will look on the one whom they have pierced.”
Thus far the Lord has helped us.
At Mizpah Israel fasts and confesses (1 Samuel 7:6); the Ebenezer stone (7:12) is a Mid-Lent milestone: God has carried us to the halfway point.
The rock was Christ.
1 Corinthians 10:4 reads the desert journey as a figure of the Christian life, nourished by spiritual food and drink.
fathers: St John Chrysostom

There the bronze serpent healed bodies from the bite of serpents; here the Crucified heals souls from the bite of the devil. There the image of a serpent, here the Lord in the likeness of sinful flesh, yet without sin (Homilies on John 27, in substance).
St Gregory of Nyssa
Moses' serpent teaches that we are freed from the poison of sin by looking to the mystery of the Passion, to the One who took the form of our sin (Life of Moses II, in substance).
magis: Catechism 2130
The bronze serpent was one of the images God permitted that pointed ahead to the Incarnation and the Cross.
Catechism 1505
By his Passion and death on the Cross Christ gave new meaning to suffering; it can unite us with his redemptive Passion.
Catechism 617–618
The Cross is the unique sacrifice of Christ, and he calls his disciples to take up their cross and follow him.
outline: Opening
Ask: when you are tired halfway through a journey, what helps you keep going?
Point 1 · Look and live
The bronze serpent and the Son of Man lifted up.
Point 2 · The one whom they have pierced
Mourning that heals; God so loved the world.
Point 3 · Thus far the Lord has helped us
Mizpah, the rock that is Christ, the way out.
Take-home line
“So must the Son of Man be lifted up.”
live: Look at the Cross (Numbers 21:8)
Today spend five minutes simply looking at a crucifix, at church or at home, without saying anything; then say: Lord, you did this for me.
Set up your Ebenezer (1 Samuel 7:12)
Write down three ways God has helped you in the first half of the Fast, and one resolution you will take up again for the second half.
2027-03-03.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, at the middle of this holy Fast your Church lifts up your life-giving Cross. As the bitten Israelites looked at the bronze serpent and lived, let us look at you, lifted up for us, and live. Pour out on us the spirit of compassion and supplication, that we may look on you whom our sins have pierced and turn to you with all our hearts. Thus far you have helped us; carry us through the rest of the Fast to Golgotha and to the joy of your Resurrection. To you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, be glory for ever. Amen.
altar: The Cross set up in the church and the altar of the Holy Qurbono speak of the same Sacrifice: the One lifted up on Golgotha is offered and given to us, truly present, so that we may “taste and see that the Lord is good.”

2027-03-04.title: Thursday of the fourth week of the Great Fast
readings: Hagar and Ishmael are sent away; God promises to make a nation of the boy
Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up
Love your enemies; be perfect as your heavenly Father is perfect
2027-03-04.verse: But I say to you, Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you,
theo: Today's first reading is painful. At the feast for Isaac, Sarah sees Ishmael, Hagar's son, playing with her son and demands: “Cast out this slave woman with her son; for the son of this slave woman shall not inherit along with my son Isaac.” Scripture is honest: “The matter was very distressing to Abraham on account of his son.” Ishmael was his child too. God tells Abraham that the line of promise will run through Isaac, but he does not forget the other boy: “As for the son of the slave woman, I will make a nation of him also, because he is your offspring.” Abraham rises early, puts bread and a skin of water on Hagar's shoulder, and sends her into the wilderness of Beer-sheba. This is a family torn apart by jealousy and fear of losing an inheritance, the kind of quarrel that still divides homes over land and property. Yet God's care reaches beyond the walls of Abraham's tent. The boy who is sent away is not sent away from God.

Paul gives the Corinthians a principle that would have helped Abraham's household: “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.” The Christians of Corinth knew that idols are nothing and that “there is no God but one,” and some were using that knowledge to look down on weaker believers. Paul corrects them: “anyone who loves God is known by him.” What matters is not how much I know but whether I build others up. St Augustine summed up the whole Christian life in a short line: love, and do what you will; for if the root within is love, nothing but good can grow from it (in substance). Jesus takes love to its furthest point: “You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy.’ But I say to you, Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you, so that you may be children of your Father in heaven; for he makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good.” The Father does not ration his sunshine according to merit. In this Great Fast we are asked to imitate that generosity: to pray for those who wrong us, and to greet those whom we would rather avoid. “Be perfect, therefore, as your heavenly Father is perfect.”
outline: Opening
Ask: has jealousy or an inheritance ever divided a family you know?
Point 1 · The boy who was sent away
Abraham's distress and God's promise to Ishmael.
Point 2 · Love builds up
Knowledge without love puffs up.
Point 3 · Love your enemies
The sun on the evil and the good.
Take-home line
“Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you.”
live: Pray for an enemy (Matthew 5:44)
Name before God one person who has hurt you or works against you, and pray for his or her good every day of this week.
Build up, do not puff up (1 Corinthians 8:1)
Today, instead of correcting or showing what you know, say one word that encourages a person who is weak or struggling.
2027-03-04.prayer: Heavenly Father, you make your sun rise on the evil and on the good and send rain on the righteous and the unrighteous. You did not forget the boy who was sent into the wilderness. Heal the jealousy and quarrels that divide our families. Keep us from the knowledge that puffs up, and fill us with the love that builds up. Give us grace in this Great Fast to love our enemies and pray for those who persecute us, so that we may be your children and grow perfect as you are perfect. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.
altar: At the altar Christ offers himself for friends and enemies alike; the love that prayed “Father, forgive them” becomes our food in the Holy Qurbono.

2027-03-05.title: Friday of the fourth week of the Great Fast · Anniversary of the enthronement of our Major Archbishop-Catholicos
2027-03-05.readTitle: Readings of the day (Syro-Malankara Panchangam; the Gospel verses are unclear in the source and are read here as John 10:14–16, verify locally)
readings: God hears the boy in the wilderness
Stand firm in your faith; let all that you do be done in love
I am the good shepherd; other sheep I have
2027-03-05.alt: Great Fast (Valiya Nombu), fourth week. Anniversary of the enthronement of Moran Mor Baselios Cardinal Cleemis Catholicos as Major Archbishop-Catholicos (2007). The Panchangam's Gospel reference for this day is unclear in the source text (it may be John 10:1–16 or John 10:14–16); check your parish lectionary. For many families it is also the First Friday of the month.
2027-03-05.verse: Do not be afraid; for God has heard the voice of the boy where he is.
theo: Yesterday Hagar and Ishmael were sent into the wilderness; today we follow them there. The water runs out. Hagar lays the boy under a bush and goes a bowshot away, “for she said, ‘Do not let me look on the death of the child.’ And as she sat opposite him, she lifted up her voice and wept.” It is one of the loneliest scenes in the Bible: a foreign slave woman, cast out, with a dying child, in a desert. And then: “God heard the voice of the boy; and the angel of God called to Hagar from heaven, and said to her, ‘What troubles you, Hagar? Do not be afraid; for God has heard the voice of the boy where he is.’” The name Ishmael means “God hears.” God hears him not after he is brought back to Abraham's tent, but “where he is,” under the bush in the desert. “Then God opened her eyes and she saw a well of water.” The well had been there all along; she needed God to open her eyes. In the Great Fast many of us feel that our water skin is empty. The Lord who heard Ishmael hears us where we are.

The Gospel shows us the Shepherd who hears and knows: “I am the good shepherd. I know my own and my own know me, just as the Father knows me and I know the Father. And I lay down my life for the sheep. I have other sheep that do not belong to this fold. I must bring them also, and they will listen to my voice. So there will be one flock, one shepherd.” Ishmael was outside the tent, but not outside God's care; Christ's heart reaches the sheep outside the fold, and he lays down his life to gather them. St Gregory the Great taught that “I know my own” means: I love them; and “my own know me” means: they obey me in love, for one who does not love does not yet truly know (in substance). Today our Church gives thanks for the anniversary of the enthronement of our Major Archbishop-Catholicos, Moran Mor Baselios Cardinal Cleemis, in 2007. We pray that he may be a shepherd after the heart of Christ, who knows his flock and seeks those far away. And Paul's farewell to the Corinthians becomes our prayer for all shepherds and for ourselves: “Keep alert, stand firm in your faith, be courageous, be strong. Let all that you do be done in love.” He ends with the ancient cry of the Church in Aramaic, which the NRSV renders: “Our Lord, come!”
outline: Opening
Ask: have you ever felt that no one could hear you?
Point 1 · God has heard the voice of the boy
Hagar's tears and the well in the desert.
Point 2 · Stand firm, do all in love
Paul's farewell and the cry “Our Lord, come!”
Point 3 · One flock, one shepherd
The Good Shepherd and our Catholicos.
Take-home line
“God has heard the voice of the boy where he is.”
live: Let God open your eyes (Genesis 21:19)
In a situation where you feel dry and helpless, ask God today to show you the “well” that is already near you: a person, a sacrament, a word of Scripture.
Pray for our shepherd (John 10:14)
Pray today for our Major Archbishop-Catholicos on the anniversary of his enthronement, and for your own bishop and parish priest.
2027-03-05.prayer: God who hears, you heard the voice of the boy Ishmael under the bush in the wilderness, and you opened Hagar's eyes to see the well of water. Hear us where we are, in our dryness and our fears. Lord Jesus, Good Shepherd, you know your own and lay down your life for them; bring home the sheep that are far away, and make us one flock under one shepherd. Bless our Major Archbishop-Catholicos, Moran Mor Baselios Cardinal Cleemis, on the anniversary of his enthronement; keep him alert and firm in faith, courageous and strong, doing all things in love. Our Lord, come! Amen.
altar: On this Friday of the Fast the Good Shepherd who laid down his life is offered at the altar; the Church's prayer “Our Lord, come!” is answered each time he comes, truly present, in the Holy Qurbono.

2027-03-06.title: Saturday of the fourth week of the Great Fast
readings: The covenant at Beer-sheba; Abraham calls on the Everlasting God
Everything created by God is good, received with thanksgiving
I must proclaim the good news to the other cities also
2027-03-06.alt: Great Fast (Valiya Nombu), fourth week. Tomorrow is K'piphtho Sunday, the fifth Sunday of the Great Fast.
2027-03-06.verse: I must proclaim the good news of the kingdom of God to the other cities also; for I was sent for this purpose.
theo: The first reading closes the week of Abraham's story with a scene of peace. Abimelech, the same king Abraham once feared, comes to him with the commander of his army and says: “God is with you in all that you do.” A pagan ruler recognizes God's presence in Abraham's life, and asks for a covenant of loyalty. There is still a dispute: Abimelech's servants have seized a well. Wells meant life in that dry land, and quarrels over water were bitter. Abraham does not fight; he sets apart seven ewe lambs as a witness that he dug the well, and the two men swear an oath. The place is named Beer-sheba, the well of the oath or the well of seven. Then, in a land that was not yet his, Abraham “planted a tamarisk tree in Beer-sheba, and called there on the name of the Lord, the Everlasting God.” A tree takes years to give shade; planting it is an act of hope. Abraham, still “an alien many days in the land of the Philistines,” lives as a guest who trusts that the Everlasting God will keep his promise.

Paul's words to Timothy are especially fitting in the Great Fast. Some false teachers, he says, “forbid marriage and demand abstinence from foods, which God created to be received with thanksgiving by those who believe and know the truth. For everything created by God is good, and nothing is to be rejected, provided it is received with thanksgiving; for it is sanctified by God’s word and by prayer.” Our fasting is not a rejection of God's good creation. We do not abstain from meat, fish or eggs because they are evil, but because we want to hunger more for God, to share with the poor, and to master our desires. St Basil the Great said that the true fast is to be a stranger to evil: to restrain the tongue, to put away anger, to stop lying and slander; fasting from food without fasting from sin is not enough (in substance). And when the Fast ends, we will receive God's gifts again with thanksgiving. In the Gospel, the crowds want to keep Jesus for themselves, but he says: “I must proclaim the good news of the kingdom of God to the other cities also; for I was sent for this purpose.” Our Lenten prayer is not meant to make us comfortable in one place. It sends us out, like Jesus, to bring the good news further, to the next village, the next house, the next person who has not heard.
outline: Opening
Ask: what do you think fasting is really for?
Point 1 · The well of the oath
Abraham makes peace and plants a tree of hope.
Point 2 · Received with thanksgiving
Why we fast from good things.
Point 3 · To the other cities also
Jesus will not be kept in one place.
Take-home line
“I must proclaim the good news of the kingdom of God to the other cities also.”
live: Make peace over a 'well' (Genesis 21:25–27)
If there is a dispute in your family or neighbourhood over water, a boundary or money, take one step this week to settle it peacefully.
Give thanks before every meal (1 Timothy 4:4–5)
During the rest of the Fast, never eat without first thanking God, and set aside what you save by fasting for someone in need.
2027-03-06.prayer: Everlasting God, Abraham called on your name under the tamarisk tree at Beer-sheba, a guest in a land that was not yet his. Make us peacemakers who settle quarrels without violence, and pilgrims who plant seeds of hope. Teach us to fast not out of contempt for your good creation but out of hunger for you, and to receive all your gifts with thanksgiving. Send us, like your Son, to bring the good news to the other cities also. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.
altar: The Holy Qurbono is the great thanksgiving: the bread and wine, good gifts of creation, are offered with prayer and become, by the power of the Holy Spirit, the Body and Blood of Christ.

2027-03-08.title: Monday of the fifth week of the Great Fast
readings: God tests Abraham: “God himself will provide the lamb”
Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ; reverence in worship
When the bridegroom is taken away, they will fast
2027-03-08.alt: Great Fast (Valiya Nombu), fifth week. The week after K'piphtho Sunday, the Sunday of the healing of the bent woman.
2027-03-08.verse: Abraham said, “God himself will provide the lamb for a burnt offering, my son.” So the two of them walked on together.
theo: Today we begin the most solemn page of Abraham's life. “After these things God tested Abraham. He said to him, ‘Abraham!’ And he said, ‘Here I am.’” Then comes the command no father could bear to hear: “Take your son, your only son Isaac, whom you love, and go to the land of Moriah, and offer him there as a burnt offering.” Abraham does not argue, as he argued for Sodom. He rises early, cuts the wood and walks for three days. Then the narrator slows down: “Abraham took the wood of the burnt offering and laid it on his son Isaac, and he himself carried the fire and the knife. So the two of them walked on together.” Isaac asks the question that hangs over the whole Old Testament: “The fire and the wood are here, but where is the lamb for a burnt offering?” And Abraham answers with a faith larger than he knows: “God himself will provide the lamb for a burnt offering, my son.” The Letter to the Hebrews says that Abraham “considered the fact that God is able even to raise someone from the dead.”

The Church has always read this story with her eyes on Golgotha. St Melito of Sardis taught that Isaac carrying the wood up the mountain was a figure of Christ carrying his Cross, and that the ram caught in the thicket pointed to the Lamb who would be offered in our place (in substance). What Abraham was spared, the Father did not spare himself: he gave his only Son, whom he loves. In the Gospel the disciples of John and of the Pharisees ask why Jesus' disciples do not fast. Jesus answers: “You cannot make wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them, can you? The days will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them, and then they will fast in those days.” Our Great Fast lives in those days: we fast because the Bridegroom was taken away to the Cross, and we fast in hope because he will come again. And the fast is not a patch on an old garment; it is new wine that needs a new heart. St Paul gives a simple rule for the new life: “Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ.” He praises the Corinthians for keeping “the traditions just as I handed them on to you,” and asks for order and reverence when the Church gathers to pray. The customs of veiling belonged to the Corinth of his day, and many women in our Church still cover their heads in prayer as a sign of reverence; but the heart of his teaching is that “in the Lord woman is not independent of man or man independent of woman,” and “all things come from God.”
outline: Opening
Ask: what is the hardest thing God has ever asked of you?
Point 1 · “Here I am”
Abraham's obedience in the dark.
Point 2 · The wood on Isaac's shoulders
A figure of Christ carrying his Cross.
Point 3 · When the bridegroom is taken away
Why the Church fasts.
Take-home line
“God himself will provide the lamb for a burnt offering, my son.”
live: Say “Here I am” (Genesis 22:1)
Begin each day this week with three words: Here I am, Lord. Then do the first duty of the day without complaint.
Fast for the Bridegroom (Luke 5:35)
Choose one small, hidden fast for the rest of this week and offer it in memory of Christ's Passion.
2027-03-08.prayer: Lord God, you tested Abraham and he answered, Here I am. You did not let him lose his son, but you did not spare your own Son and gave him up for us all. Give us Abraham's trust when your ways are dark, let us walk with Christ as Isaac walked with his father, and keep our fast as the friends of the Bridegroom, until he comes again. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.
altar: On the altar of the Holy Qurbono the Lamb whom God himself provided is offered for us, once for all, and given to us as food.

2027-03-09.title: Tuesday of the fifth week of the Great Fast · The Forty Martyrs of Sebaste
readings: “The Lord will provide”: the ram in place of Isaac
Completing what is lacking in Christ's afflictions for the sake of his body
Take up your cross and follow me
2027-03-09.alt: Great Fast (Valiya Nombu), fifth week. Commemoration of the Forty Martyrs of Sebaste.
2027-03-09.verse: He called the crowd with his disciples, and said to them, “If any want to become my followers, let them deny themselves and take up their cross and follow me.
theo: Yesterday we left Abraham and Isaac walking up the mountain together. Today the story reaches its summit. “Abraham built an altar there and laid the wood in order. He bound his son Isaac, and laid him on the altar, on top of the wood.” At the last moment the angel calls: “Do not lay your hand on the boy or do anything to him; for now I know that you fear God, since you have not withheld your son, your only son, from me.” Abraham sees a ram caught in a thicket and offers it “instead of his son,” and he names the place “The Lord will provide.” God then swears by himself: “by your offspring shall all the nations of the earth gain blessing for themselves, because you have obeyed my voice.” St Paul hears the echo of this chapter when he writes: “He who did not withhold his own Son, but gave him up for all of us, will he not with him also give us everything else?” Isaac was spared; the Son of God was not. Tradition places Moriah where the Temple later stood, near the hill where Christ was crucified, so that the mountain of the test became the mountain of the gift.

In the Gospel Jesus speaks openly of that gift: “the Son of Man must undergo great suffering, and be rejected… and be killed, and after three days rise again.” Peter, who had just confessed him as the Messiah, takes him aside to rebuke him, and Jesus answers: “Get behind me, Satan! For you are setting your mind not on divine things but on human things.” Then he speaks to all: “If any want to become my followers, let them deny themselves and take up their cross and follow me.” Today the Church remembers forty soldiers who did exactly that. At Sebaste in Armenia, around the year 320, under the emperor Licinius, forty Christian soldiers refused to sacrifice to idols. They were left naked through a winter night on a frozen lake, with a warm bath-house on the shore for anyone who would deny Christ. One gave up and ran to the bath; a guard, seeing the faith of the others, took off his own clothes and joined them, so that forty still stood on the ice. St Basil the Great, preaching on their feast, imagined them praying: the winter is bitter, but paradise is sweet; the frost is painful, but the rest that follows is blessed (in substance). St Paul gives the meaning of such suffering: “I am now rejoicing in my sufferings for your sake, and in my flesh I am completing what is lacking in Christ's afflictions for the sake of his body, that is, the church.” Nothing is lacking in Christ's sacrifice; what remains is for his members to share in it, so that his love reaches every place and age.
outline: Opening
Ask: what would make me turn back on a cold night?
Point 1 · On the mount of the Lord
The ram in Isaac's place; the Son not withheld.
Point 2 · Take up your cross
Peter's human thinking and the way of Jesus.
Point 3 · Forty on the ice
Completing what is lacking for the sake of the Church.
Take-home line
“Let them deny themselves and take up their cross and follow me.”
live: Do not withhold (Genesis 22:12)
Name one thing you have kept back from God this Lent and offer it to him today in prayer.
Take up your cross (Mark 8:34)
Accept one discomfort today without complaint and unite it to Christ for someone who is suffering.
2027-03-09.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, the Father did not withhold you from us but gave you up for us all, and on the mountain of the Lord he provided the Lamb. You call us to deny ourselves, take up our cross and follow you. By the prayers of the Forty Martyrs of Sebaste, who stood firm through the frozen night, give us courage not to turn back toward easy comfort, and let our small sufferings serve your body, the Church. Amen.
altar: The sacrifice that Abraham was spared, the Father offered in his Son; at the altar of the Holy Qurbono we share in it and receive the strength of the martyrs.

2027-03-10.title: Wednesday of the fifth week of the Great Fast
readings: The children of Nahor; Rebekah's family
Elders who rule well are worthy of double honour
2027-03-10.verse: I have compassion for the crowd, because they have been with me now for three days and have nothing to eat;
theo: After the drama of Moriah, Genesis seems to change the subject: “Now after these things it was told Abraham, ‘Milcah also has borne children, to your brother Nahor.’” A list of names follows, and among them one short sentence: “Bethuel became the father of Rebekah.” It is easy to skip, but it is the hinge of the next chapter. While Abraham was climbing the mountain with Isaac, God was already preparing, far away in Haran, the girl who would one day be Isaac's wife and the mother of Jacob. God's promises do not move forward only through visions and angels; they move through births, families and ordinary news. St Paul says that “when the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman”; the long genealogies of the Bible are the patient road by which that fullness came. No family is too ordinary to be part of God's plan.

The Gospel shows the same God, now in the flesh, caring for ordinary needs. “I have compassion for the crowd, because they have been with me now for three days and have nothing to eat; and I do not want to send them away hungry, for they might faint on the way.” The disciples see only the desert: “Where are we to get enough bread in the desert to feed so great a crowd?” Jesus asks what they have, “Seven, and a few small fish,” and then does what he will do at the Last Supper: “he took the seven loaves and the fish; and after giving thanks he broke them and gave them to the disciples, and the disciples gave them to the crowds.” Many Fathers noted that this second feeding took place among people from the Gentile side of the lake, a sign that the Bread of Life is for all nations. Notice the order: Christ gives to the disciples, and the disciples give to the people. That is the ministry of the priest at the Holy Qurbono, and it is why the Letter to Timothy says: “Let the elders who rule well be considered worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in preaching and teaching.” The same passage asks for justice (“Never accept any accusation against an elder except on the evidence of two or three witnesses”) and for great care in choosing them: “Do not ordain anyone hastily.” St Ignatius of Antioch urged the faithful to respect their presbyters as the council of God and the college of the apostles (in substance). To honour our priests is to honour the Lord who feeds us through their hands; to pray for them is to share in their work.
outline: Opening
Ask: who fed you with the word of God when you were young?
Point 1 · Bethuel became the father of Rebekah
God quietly prepares the future.
Point 2 · Double honour
Priests who labour in preaching and teaching.
Point 3 · I have compassion
Seven loaves, thanksgiving, breaking, giving.
Take-home line
“I have compassion for the crowd.”
live: Honour your priests (1 Timothy 5:17)
Thank a priest of your parish this week in person or with a short note, and pray for him by name each day.
Share what you have (Matthew 15:34)
Give from your own food this week to someone who has little, as the disciples gave the seven loaves.
2027-03-10.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you had compassion on the hungry crowd and fed them with seven loaves, giving thanks, breaking and giving through your disciples. Bless the priests who give us your word and your Body and Blood; keep them holy, guard them from injustice, and send good workers into your harvest. As you prepared Rebekah's family long before she was needed, prepare our families for your plan. Amen.
altar: At the altar Christ still takes the bread, gives thanks, breaks it and gives it through the hands of his priests, so that no one need faint on the way.

2027-03-11.title: Thursday of the fifth week of the Great Fast
readings: Sarah dies; Abraham, a stranger, asks for a burial place
The hope laid up for you in heaven
No sign but the sign of Jonah
2027-03-11.verse: I am a stranger and an alien residing among you; give me property among you for a burying place, so that I may bury my dead out of my sight.
theo: “Sarah lived one hundred twenty-seven years… And Sarah died at Kiriath-arba (that is, Hebron) in the land of Canaan; and Abraham went in to mourn for Sarah and to weep for her.” The man who did not weep on Mount Moriah weeps now beside his wife. Scripture does not hide his tears; faith does not forbid grief, it gives grief a direction. Then Abraham “rose up from beside his dead” and spoke to the Hittites: “I am a stranger and an alien residing among you; give me property among you for a burying place.” After more than sixty years in the land God had promised him, Abraham does not own a single field. The promise is real, but it is still ahead. The Hittites answer him with honour, “you are a mighty prince among us,” and Abraham bows before “the people of the land.” The father of believers deals courteously and justly with people of another nation and another faith, a lesson our multi-religious land knows well. The Letter to the Hebrews explains his patience: the patriarchs “died in faith without having received the promises… They confessed that they were strangers and foreigners on the earth.” An early Christian writer, the author of the Letter to Diognetus, said the same of Christians: they live in their own countries, but as sojourners; every foreign land is a homeland to them, and every homeland a foreign land (in substance).

St Paul tells the Colossians where the Christian homeland is: “we always thank God… for we have heard of your faith in Christ Jesus and of the love that you have for all the saints, because of the hope laid up for you in heaven.” Faith, love and hope: hope is the treasure stored up ahead, and it gives strength to faith and love today. That is why we can grieve without despair, as Paul says elsewhere, “so that you may not grieve as others do who have no hope.” Our Church prays for the departed at every Holy Qurbono, and in the Great Fast we remember them with special love. In the Gospel the Pharisees and Sadducees ask Jesus for “a sign from heaven.” He answers that they can read the sky, red at evening, red in the morning, “but you cannot interpret the signs of the times.” And he gives them only one sign: “An evil and adulterous generation asks for a sign, but no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah.” Jonah came out of the sea monster after three days; Jesus will come out of the tomb on the third day. The Resurrection is the sign that answers Abraham's grave, Sarah's death and every Christian funeral. In three weeks we will sing it at Easter.
outline: Opening
Ask: where is my true home?
Point 1 · Abraham wept for Sarah
Faith gives grief a direction.
Point 2 · A stranger and an alien
Living in the land of promise without owning it.
Point 3 · The sign of Jonah
Hope laid up in heaven, proved by the empty tomb.
Take-home line
“I am a stranger and an alien residing among you.”
live: Pray for the departed (Genesis 23:2)
Visit a cemetery or pray at home this week for a departed member of your family, and have a Holy Qurbono offered for them if you can.
Read the signs of the times (Matthew 16:3)
Spend ten minutes this week asking what God is saying to you through the events around you, and write one line about it.
2027-03-11.prayer: Lord God, Abraham wept for Sarah and lived as a stranger in the land you promised him, trusting in a better country. Comfort all who mourn, give eternal rest to our departed, and keep our eyes on the hope laid up for us in heaven. Give us the one sign that is enough, the sign of Jonah, your Son risen from the tomb. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.
altar: At every Holy Qurbono the Church remembers her departed and offers the sacrifice of the One who came out of the tomb on the third day.

2027-03-12.title: Friday of the fifth week of the Great Fast
readings: Abraham pays the full price for the field of Ephron
Christ is our peace: the dividing wall broken down
Beware the yeast; do you not yet understand?
2027-03-12.alt: Great Fast (Valiya Nombu), fifth week. A Friday of the Great Fast: abstinence and the Way of the Cross, as is the custom of our parishes. Next Friday, 19 March, is the Fortieth Friday.
2027-03-12.verse: For he is our peace; in his flesh he has made both groups into one and has broken down the dividing wall, that is, the hostility between us.
theo: The negotiation at Hebron is told in slow, careful detail, at the city gate, “in the hearing of the Hittites.” Ephron makes a generous public offer: “No, my lord, hear me; I give you the field, and I give you the cave that is in it… bury your dead.” Abraham bows, and refuses the gift: “I will give the price of the field; accept it from me, so that I may bury my dead there.” Ephron names the price as if it were nothing, “four hundred shekels of silver, what is that between you and me?”, and Abraham pays it in full, “according to the weights current among the merchants.” Why does Genesis care so much? Because this is the first piece of the promised land that belongs to Abraham, and it must be his openly, justly and beyond dispute. He will not hold God's promise on a borrowed title or leave a debt behind his wife's grave. Centuries later King David says the same when he buys the threshing floor for the altar: “I will not offer burnt offerings to the Lord my God that cost me nothing.” Honest dealing in money and property is part of holiness, and the Great Fast is a good time to set right any unpaid debt, unfair price or unclear boundary.

Abraham bought a field with silver; Christ bought a people with his blood. St Paul reminds the Christians of Ephesus, Gentiles by birth, that they were once “without Christ, being aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope and without God in the world. But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ. For he is our peace.” The dividing wall that Christ broke down is the hostility between peoples, and above all between each of us and God; on the Cross he reconciled “both groups to God in one body.” The Gentiles do not replace Israel; they are brought near to share its promises, “citizens with the saints and also members of the household of God, built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus himself as the cornerstone.” St John Chrysostom compared this to melting a statue of silver and a statue of lead together and drawing out from the fire a single statue of gold: Christ does not merely put two peoples side by side but makes of them something new (in substance). In the Gospel the disciples have “only one loaf with them in the boat,” and when Jesus warns them, “beware of the yeast of the Pharisees and the yeast of Herod,” they think only of bread. Yeast is a small hidden thing that spreads through the whole batch: the leaven of hardness of heart and of worldly power can enter any of us. Jesus asks: “Are your hearts hardened? Do you have eyes, and fail to see?… Do you not yet understand?” The one Loaf in the boat was Jesus himself, who had fed thousands and would give his Body on the Cross.
outline: Opening
Ask: is there a debt or a wrong I have left unsettled?
Point 1 · For the full price
Abraham's honest purchase of the field.
Point 2 · He is our peace
The dividing wall broken down by the Cross.
Point 3 · The one loaf in the boat
Beware the yeast; do you not yet understand?
Take-home line
“For he is our peace.”
live: Settle accounts (Genesis 23:16)
Before Easter, pay one debt, return one borrowed thing, or set right one unfair deal.
Break down a wall (Ephesians 2:14)
Make peace this week with one person or family with whom you have a quarrel.
2027-03-12.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, by your blood you brought near those who were far off, and on the Cross you broke down the dividing wall of hostility.
