Make us honest in our dealings like Abraham, peacemakers in our homes and parishes, and free from the yeast of hypocrisy and the love of power. Open our eyes to see you, the one Bread in our boat. Amen.
altar: At the altar the Body broken on the Cross makes us one body, reconciled to God and to one another.

2027-03-13.title: Saturday of the fifth week of the Great Fast
readings: The field and cave of Machpelah become Abraham's; Sarah is buried
Boasting excluded; justified by faith; we uphold the law
You are my friends; I chose you
2027-03-13.alt: Great Fast (Valiya Nombu), fifth week. Anniversary of the episcopal ordination (2010) of the Most Rev. Vincent Mar Paulos, Thomas Mar Antonios, Samuel Mar Irenios and Philipose Mar Stephanos. Tomorrow is Samio Sunday, the Sunday of the healing of the blind man.
2027-03-13.verse: No one has greater love than this, to lay down one’s life for one’s friends.
theo: The story of the field at Hebron ends with a legal formula repeated twice: “So the field of Ephron in Machpelah… the field with the cave that was in it and all the trees that were in the field… passed to Abraham as a possession.” Then, simply: “After this, Abraham buried Sarah his wife in the cave of the field of Machpelah facing Mamre (that is, Hebron) in the land of Canaan.” The first part of the promised land that Abraham owns is a tomb. Later Abraham himself will be laid there, and Isaac and Rebekah, and Jacob and Leah. It looks like a sad ending, but it is an act of hope. To bury your dead in the land of promise is to say: God will keep his word, even beyond death. The Letter to the Hebrews says of the patriarchs: “they desire a better country, that is, a heavenly one. Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God.” Christian cemeteries carry the same faith; we call them places of sleep, because we await the resurrection of the body.

St Paul asks: “Then what becomes of boasting? It is excluded. By what law? By that of works? No, but by the law of faith. For we hold that a person is justified by faith apart from works prescribed by the law.” Abraham did not earn the promise; he received it and trusted it, even to the grave. Paul means that no one is made righteous by the observances of the Mosaic law, and the Church teaches that justification is God's free gift, received in faith and baptism, which then bears fruit in love; so no one can boast. And Paul adds at once: “Is he not the God of Gentiles also? Yes… since God is one,” and “Do we then overthrow the law by this faith? By no means! On the contrary, we uphold the law.” The law is fulfilled in the commandment Jesus gives in the Gospel: “This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you. No one has greater love than this, to lay down one’s life for one’s friends.” He calls us friends, not servants, and he reminds us whose initiative it was: “You did not choose me but I chose you. And I appointed you to go and bear fruit, fruit that will last.” St Augustine commented that Christ did not choose us because we were good; he chose us so that we might become good (in substance). Today we give thanks for four shepherds of our Church, Vincent Mar Paulos, Thomas Mar Antonios, Samuel Mar Irenios and Philipose Mar Stephanos, ordained bishops on this day in 2010: chosen and appointed to bear fruit that will last. Tomorrow, on Samio Sunday, the Lord opens the eyes of the blind.
outline: Opening
Ask: what is my hope built on?
Point 1 · A tomb in the land of promise
Machpelah, a burial in hope.
Point 2 · Boasting excluded
Justified by faith, the law upheld.
Point 3 · I chose you
Friends who lay down their lives and bear fruit.
Take-home line
“No one has greater love than this, to lay down one's life for one's friends.”
live: Hope beyond the grave (Genesis 23:19)
Pray this week at the grave of someone you love, or light a candle at home, and say the Creed slowly, especially “the resurrection of the body.”
Love as he loved (John 15:12)
Do one hidden act of self-giving today for someone who cannot repay you.
2027-03-13.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you laid down your life for your friends and called us friends, not servants. You chose us, not because we were good, but so that we might become good and bear fruit that will last. Exclude all boasting from our hearts, keep us in the faith of Abraham who buried his dead in hope, and bless our bishops Vincent Mar Paulos, Thomas Mar Antonios, Samuel Mar Irenios and Philipose Mar Stephanos, whom you chose and appointed for your people. Amen.
altar: At the altar the Friend who laid down his life for us gives us his Body and Blood, so that we may love one another as he has loved us.

2027-03-15.title: Monday of the sixth week of the Great Fast
readings: Abraham sends his servant to find a wife for Isaac
Pray in the Spirit at all times; an ambassador in chains
“By what authority are you doing these things?”
2027-03-15.alt: Great Fast (Valiya Nombu), sixth week. The last full week of the Forty Days: the Fortieth Friday is 19 March, Lazarus Saturday 20 March, and Hosanna Sunday 21 March.
2027-03-15.verse: Pray in the Spirit at all times in every prayer and supplication. To that end keep alert and always persevere in supplication for all the saints.
theo: This week the readings from Genesis follow one long and lovely story: how Abraham's servant went to find a bride for Isaac. It begins today with an old man settling his affairs. “Now Abraham was old, well advanced in years; and the Lord had blessed Abraham in all things.” He calls the oldest servant of his house and makes him swear that he will not take a wife for Isaac from the Canaanites around them, but will go back to Abraham's own kindred. The servant raises an honest difficulty: what if the woman will not come? Abraham's answer is the answer of a man who has walked with God for a lifetime: “The Lord, the God of heaven, who took me from my father’s house and from the land of my birth, and who spoke to me and swore to me, ‘To your offspring I will give this land,’ he will send his angel before you.” Abraham cannot see how it will work out; he only knows who has been faithful to him. The promise of descendants as many as the stars depends on this one marriage, and Abraham entrusts it to God. Isaac must not go back: the family of promise looks forward, not backward.

Paul, writing from prison, asks the Ephesians for the same trust expressed as prayer: “Pray in the Spirit at all times in every prayer and supplication. To that end keep alert and always persevere in supplication for all the saints.” He calls himself “an ambassador in chains,” and asks them to pray that he may speak the mystery of the gospel boldly. In the Gospel Jesus stands in the Temple in the last days before his Passion, and the authorities demand: “By what authority are you doing these things? Who gave you this authority to do them?” Jesus answers with a question about John the Baptist, and they will not answer, not because they do not know, but because they fear the crowd. St John Chrysostom remarked that the Lord does not hide the truth from those who seek it, but he does not cast it before those who ask only to trap him (in substance). As the Forty Days draw to a close, the Church asks us whether we come to Jesus to argue or to obey. His authority is the authority of the Son, and in a few days it will be shown most clearly on the Cross.
outline: Opening
Ask: when you cannot see the way ahead, whom do you trust?
Point 1 · He will send his angel before you
Abraham trusts the God who has been faithful.
Point 2 · Pray at all times
An ambassador in chains asks for prayer.
Point 3 · By what authority?
Coming to Jesus to obey, not to argue.
Take-home line
“Pray in the Spirit at all times.”
live: Entrust the future (Genesis 24:7)
Name one decision that worries you, and give it to God in prayer each morning this week.
Pray for the ambassadors (Ephesians 6:19)
Pray every day this week for one priest or missionary by name, that he or she may speak the gospel boldly.
2027-03-15.prayer: Lord God of heaven and earth, you led Abraham from his father's house and sent your angel before his servant. Go before us in the choices we must make, and teach us to trust you where we cannot see. Keep us alert and persevering in prayer for all your saints, and give courage to all who proclaim your gospel, especially those in chains. Let us come to your Son not to argue but to obey, as we follow him to Jerusalem. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.
altar: Abraham trusted that God would provide; at the altar the Father gives us the Bridegroom himself, the Son with all authority, given for the life of the world.

2027-03-16.title: Tuesday of the sixth week of the Great Fast
readings: The servant prays at the well
Christ in you, the hope of glory
2027-03-16.verse: To them God chose to make known how great among the Gentiles are the riches of the glory of this mystery, which is Christ in you, the hope of glory.
theo: Abraham's servant sets out with ten camels and choice gifts and travels to Aram-naharaim, to the city of Nahor. “He made the camels kneel down outside the city by the well of water; it was toward evening, the time when women go out to draw water.” There, before doing anything else, he prays. It is the first prayer for guidance recorded in the Bible: “O Lord, God of my master Abraham, please grant me success today and show steadfast love to my master Abraham.” Then he asks for a sign, and the sign he asks for is wise. He does not ask for the most beautiful girl or the richest family. He asks for a heart: the girl who, when a tired stranger asks for a drink, will say, “Drink, and I will water your camels.” Ten thirsty camels after a desert journey would need a great deal of water drawn by hand. Only a generous, hard-working and kind young woman would offer that. The servant knows that what makes a good wife and mother in Israel is not wealth but a heart like God's own, quick to serve. Before a great decision he kneels his camels, stands by the spring and prays.

Paul shows a different kind of service, the service of suffering: “I am now rejoicing in my sufferings for your sake, and in my flesh I am completing what is lacking in Christ’s afflictions for the sake of his body, that is, the church.” This does not mean that the Cross of Christ was insufficient; his one sacrifice redeemed the whole world. It means that Christ, the Head, wills to share his saving work with his Body. St Augustine taught that the whole Christ is Head and members, and that what Christ suffered in his own flesh is filled up in the sufferings of his members until the end of time (in substance). That is why the Lord said to Saul, “why do you persecute me?” And the heart of it all is “Christ in you, the hope of glory.” In the Gospel Jesus tells his disciples a second time: “The Son of Man is to be betrayed into human hands, and they will kill him, and three days after being killed, he will rise again.” Mark adds, sadly: “they did not understand what he was saying and were afraid to ask him.” Holy Week is near. Let us not be afraid to ask him what his Cross means for our lives.
outline: Opening
Ask: before a big decision, what do you do first?
Point 1 · Prayer at the well
The servant asks for a generous heart.
Point 2 · Rejoicing in sufferings
Christ shares his saving work with his Body.
Point 3 · Afraid to ask
Bringing our questions about the Cross to Jesus.
Take-home line
“Christ in you, the hope of glory.”
live: Pray first (Genesis 24:12)
Before any important conversation or decision this week, stop and pray one sentence: Lord, grant me success today.
Offer your suffering (Colossians 1:24)
Choose one pain or difficulty you are carrying and offer it each day this week for the Church, naming a person who needs grace.
2027-03-16.prayer: Lord God of Abraham, your servant prayed at the well and you heard him before he had finished speaking. Teach us to pray before we choose, and give us generous hearts that serve beyond what is asked. Unite our sufferings with the afflictions of your Son for the sake of his Body, the Church. Let Christ dwell in us, our hope of glory, and do not let us be afraid to ask him the meaning of his Cross. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.
altar: At the altar the Head offers himself, and his Body, the Church, offers with him every suffering joined to his: the whole Christ before the Father.

2027-03-17.title: Wednesday of the sixth week of the Great Fast · St Patrick
readings: Rebekah at the well: “I will draw for your camels also”
Be imitators of God, as beloved children
“The Spirit of the Lord is upon me”
2027-03-17.alt: Great Fast (Valiya Nombu), sixth week. Commemoration of St Patrick, bishop, apostle of Ireland.
2027-03-17.verse: Therefore be imitators of God, as beloved children, and live in love, as Christ loved us and gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God.
theo: God answers the servant's prayer at once: “Before he had finished speaking, there was Rebekah,” coming out with her water jar on her shoulder. He runs to her and asks for a little water. Watch how she answers: “Drink, my lord,” she says, and “quickly” lowers her jar; then, without being asked, “I will draw for your camels also, until they have finished drinking.” She empties her jar into the trough and runs again to the well, again and again, until all ten camels have drunk. The text is full of her speed: quickly, ran, quickly. Her generosity is not measured; it goes to the end. The servant “gazed at her in silence,” and when he learns that she is of Abraham's kindred, he bows his head and worships: “Blessed be the Lord, the God of my master Abraham, who has not forsaken his steadfast love and his faithfulness toward my master.” Origen loved this scene. He noted that Rebekah came to the wells every day, and that is why the servant of Abraham found her there; so the soul that comes daily to the wells of Scripture will meet the messenger of the Bridegroom (in substance).

Paul tells us whose generosity Rebekah reflects: “be imitators of God, as beloved children, and live in love, as Christ loved us and gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God.” Christ did not give a measured love; he gave himself, to the end, and that self-offering is made present on our altar in every Holy Qurbono. In the Gospel, Jesus goes to the synagogue at Nazareth “on the sabbath day, as was his custom,” and reads from Isaiah: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to bring good news to the poor. He has sent me to proclaim release to the captives.” Today we remember St Patrick, who knew captivity from the inside. Seized from Britain by raiders at about sixteen, he spent six years as a slave herding flocks in Ireland, and there, he tells us in his Confession, he learned to pray many times a day and through the night (in substance). He escaped, became a priest and bishop, and then did the most Christ-like thing: he went back to the land of his slavery to bring the people who had enslaved him the good news of release. That is what it means to be an imitator of God.
outline: Opening
Ask: when did someone do more for you than you asked?
Point 1 · I will draw for your camels also
Rebekah's generosity goes to the end.
Point 2 · Imitators of God
Christ gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering.
Point 3 · Release to the captives
Patrick returns to the land of his slavery.
Take-home line
“Be imitators of God, as beloved children.”
live: Draw for the camels too (Genesis 24:19)
Today, when someone asks you for a small help, do the whole job, gladly and without being asked twice.
Go back with good news (Luke 4:18)
Think of one person who hurt you, and do one kind thing for them or pray for them by name, as Patrick did for Ireland.
2027-03-17.prayer: Lord God, you answered the servant's prayer before he had finished speaking and showed him Rebekah's generous heart. Make us imitators of you, as beloved children, living in love as Christ loved us and gave himself up for us. By the prayers of St Patrick, who returned with the gospel to the land of his captivity, give us courage to bring good news to the poor and release to captives, and to love even those who have wronged us. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.
altar: Christ “gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God”; the same offering is made present on the altar of the Holy Qurbono.

2027-03-18.title: Thursday of the sixth week of the Great Fast · Mar Cyril of Jerusalem
readings: “I will not eat until I have told my errand”
Clothe yourselves with love; let the word of Christ dwell in you richly
You are the salt of the earth and the light of the world
2027-03-18.alt: Great Fast (Valiya Nombu), sixth week. Commemoration of Mar Cyril (Koorilos), bishop of Jerusalem and doctor of the Church; name day of Archbishop Thomas Mar Koorilos.
2027-03-18.verse: Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly; teach and admonish one another in all wisdom; and with gratitude in your hearts sing psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs to God.
theo: Rebekah runs home with her news, and her brother Laban runs out to the well. Genesis notes, with a quiet smile, that he came “as soon as he had seen the nose-ring, and the bracelets on his sister’s arms.” Later chapters will show that Laban loves gold more than truth. Yet he speaks a true word: “Come in, O blessed of the Lord.” Water is brought for washing feet, the camels are fed, and food is set before the guest. Then the servant says something remarkable: “I will not eat until I have told my errand.” The mission comes before his own hunger. And when he speaks, he speaks only about his master: how the Lord has blessed Abraham, how Sarah bore a son in her old age, how Abraham sent him with an oath, and how the Lord, “before whom I walk, will send his angel with you and make your way successful.” The servant never tells us his own name. He is the model of every faithful messenger, of every catechist and bishop: he does not preach himself but the one who sent him. Jesus would say the same at another well: “My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to complete his work.”

Today the Church remembers such a messenger, Mar Cyril of Jerusalem (about 315–386). As bishop of the holy city he was exiled more than once in the storms of the Arian controversy, yet he is remembered above all for his catechesis. In Lent, in the church built over the Tomb of the Lord, he taught those preparing for baptism; in Easter week he explained the mysteries to the newly baptized. Of the Holy Qurbono he taught: do not look on the bread and wine as plain bread and wine, for by the Lord's own word they are his Body and Blood; even if your senses suggest otherwise, let faith make you sure (in substance). Paul's words today could describe Cyril's whole ministry: “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly; teach and admonish one another in all wisdom.” And his baptismal catechesis shines through Paul's image of clothing: “clothe yourselves with compassion, kindness, humility, meekness, and patience… Above all, clothe yourselves with love.” Jesus tells such disciples, “You are the salt of the earth… You are the light of the world.” Faith well taught and lived gives taste and light to everything around it. On this day we pray also for Archbishop Thomas Mar Koorilos on his name day.
outline: Opening
Ask: who taught you the faith, and what did they talk about most?
Point 1 · I will not eat until I have told my errand
The faithful messenger speaks of his master.
Point 2 · Let the word of Christ dwell in you
Mar Cyril the catechist; faith in the Eucharist.
Point 3 · Salt and light
Faith lived gives taste and light.
Take-home line
“Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly.”
live: Speak of the Master (Genesis 24:34)
This week, when you speak about your faith, speak less about yourself and more about what the Lord has done.
Let the word dwell richly (Colossians 3:16)
Read one Gospel chapter slowly each day until Easter, and share one verse with your family at supper.
2027-03-18.prayer: Lord God, the servant of Abraham would not eat until he had told his errand, and he spoke only of his master's blessing. Make us faithful messengers of your Son. By the prayers of Mar Cyril of Jerusalem, who taught catechumens beside the Tomb of the Lord, let the word of Christ dwell in us richly; deepen our faith in the Body and Blood of your Son in the Holy Qurbono; clothe us with compassion and love; and make us salt and light for the world. Bless Archbishop Thomas Mar Koorilos on his name day, and all who teach the faith. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.
altar: Mar Cyril taught that the bread and wine, by the Lord's own word, become his Body and Blood: what the eyes cannot see, faith receives.

2027-03-19.title: The Fortieth Friday · Mar Yauseph (St Joseph)
readings: Jesus fasts forty days and is tempted
David will not offer what costs him nothing
Amend your ways and your doings
Ransomed with the precious blood of Christ
Whether we live or die, we are the Lord's
Joseph did as the angel commanded
2027-03-19.alt: The Fortieth Friday: the forty days of the Great Fast (Valiya Nombu) are completed today. Also the feast of Mar Yauseph (St Joseph), spouse of the Virgin Mary, with its own readings (Romans 4:16–18; Matthew 1:18–25). The Panchangam notes that there is no fasting and no forty prostrations (kumbideel) today. Tomorrow is Lazarus Saturday, and Sunday is Hosanna Sunday: remind the faithful to bring palm leaves and flowers.
2027-03-19.verse: One does not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God.
theo: Today the forty days are complete. Since Shubkono on 8 February the Church has fasted, prayed and made her prostrations, walking with the Lord who “fasted forty days and forty nights, and afterwards he was famished.” The Panchangam sets side by side two scenes of temptation. In a garden full of fruit the serpent asks, “Did God say…?” and promises, “You will not die… you will be like God.” The woman sees that the tree is “good for food,” “a delight to the eyes,” and “to be desired to make one wise”; she takes and eats, and gives to her husband. In a desert without bread the same tempter comes to Jesus with the same three hungers: for bread, for display, for power. Where Adam doubted the word of God, Jesus answers each time with that word: “It is written, ‘One does not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God.’” St Irenaeus taught that the Lord fought as a man against the enemy who had taken us captive in Adam, and conquered him, so that what was lost at a tree in a garden was won back in obedience (in substance). Luke adds a sober line: “When the devil had finished every test, he departed from him until an opportune time.” That time will come in Gethsemane and on the Cross.

The other readings ask what our fast has been for. Isaiah hears the people complain, “Why do we fast, but you do not see?” and God answers: “Is not this the fast that I choose: to loose the bonds of injustice… Is it not to share your bread with the hungry, and bring the homeless poor into your house?” Jeremiah, at the Temple gate, warns against trusting in holy places while living unholy lives: “Amend your ways and your doings, and let me dwell with you in this place.” David, buying the threshing floor where the Temple would later stand, refuses a free gift: “I will not offer burnt offerings to the Lord my God that cost me nothing.” And Peter shows us the price of our own redemption: “not with perishable things like silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without defect or blemish.” So Paul can say: “If we live, we live to the Lord, and if we die, we die to the Lord; so then, whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord’s.” The forty days end today, but the Fast is not over: tomorrow we stand at the tomb of Lazarus, and on Sunday we enter Jerusalem with the Lord and begin the Week of the Passion.

This year the Fortieth Friday falls on the feast of Mar Yauseph, St Joseph, and so the Church does not fast or make the prostrations today. Joseph is the right companion for this day. Like Abraham, of whom Paul writes, “Hoping against hope, he believed,” Joseph trusted God's word when nothing made sense. Finding Mary with child, “being a righteous man and unwilling to expose her to public disgrace,” he planned to dismiss her quietly. Then the angel spoke in a dream: “Joseph, son of David, do not be afraid to take Mary as your wife, for the child conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit.” And Matthew gives the whole of Joseph in one line: “When Joseph awoke from sleep, he did as the angel of the Lord commanded him.” Where Adam heard God's word and doubted it, Joseph heard and obeyed at once, without a single recorded word. Pope Francis, in Patris Corde, called him a father in the shadows, beloved, tender, obedient, accepting, creatively courageous and a working man (in substance). The guardian of the Child in Bethlehem stood near the Mother at the beginning of the road that ends at Calvary. On the last day of the Forty, we ask him to guard the Church as he guarded the Holy Family.
outline: Opening
Ask: what has the Fast changed in me in these forty days?
Point 1 · Two gardens, one desert
Adam doubts the word; Christ conquers with it.
Point 2 · The fast that I choose
Mercy, amendment, a sacrifice that costs, the precious blood.
Point 3 · Joseph did as the angel commanded
Silent obedience, hoping against hope.
Take-home line
“One does not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God.”
live: Answer with the word (Matthew 4:4)
Choose one verse from today's readings and learn it by heart; say it whenever temptation comes this Holy Week.
The fast God chooses (Isaiah 58:7)
Before Sunday, give what you saved by fasting during these forty days to someone who is hungry or homeless.
Obey like Joseph (Matthew 1:24)
Do at once one thing you know God has been asking of you, without waiting for a better time.
2027-03-19.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, for forty days and forty nights you fasted in the wilderness and overcame the tempter by the word of God, where our first parents fell. Thank you for bringing us to the end of these forty days. Let our fast bear fruit in mercy to the hungry, in amended lives, and in offerings that cost us something, for you have ransomed us with your precious blood. By the prayers of Mar Yauseph, the righteous man who did at once what the Lord commanded, give us silent and ready obedience, guard our families, and lead us with you into Jerusalem, to your Cross and your Resurrection. Amen.
altar: We were ransomed “not with perishable things like silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ”; that blood, the price of our redemption, is offered and given on the altar.

2027-03-20.title: Lazarus Saturday · The Saturday of the Raising of Lazarus
readings: “Will you go with this man?” “I will.”
Christ the first fruits; the last enemy is death
2027-03-20.alt: Lazarus Saturday, between the end of the Forty Days and Hosanna Sunday. Tomorrow is Hosanna Sunday: bring palm leaves and flowers; the Week of the Passion (Hasho) begins tomorrow evening.
2027-03-20.verse: Jesus said to her, “Did I not tell you that if you believed, you would see the glory of God?”
theo: The Forty Days ended yesterday; Hosanna Sunday is tomorrow. Between them, like the Churches of the East, our Church keeps the Saturday of Lazarus. The order is the order of John's Gospel: the raising of Lazarus is the last and greatest of Jesus' signs, and it opens the road to Jerusalem. John tells us that the crowd who came out with palms came “not only because of Jesus but also to see Lazarus, whom he had raised from the dead.” Today's Gospel begins as Martha goes to call her sister: “The Teacher is here and is calling for you.” Mary rises quickly, and the friends who were consoling her follow, thinking she is going to the tomb to weep. She falls at Jesus' feet with the same words Martha had said: “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.” Then John shows us the heart of God made flesh: “When Jesus saw her weeping, and the Jews who came with her also weeping, he was greatly disturbed in spirit and deeply moved.” He asks, “Where have you laid him?” They answer, “Lord, come and see.” And “Jesus began to weep.” The mourners, neighbours and friends of the family who had come from Jerusalem to share their grief, say, “See how he loved him!” Many of them, John tells us, believed in him that day.

At the tomb, a cave with a stone across it, Jesus says, “Take away the stone.” Practical Martha protests: “Lord, already there is a stench because he has been dead four days.” Jesus answers: “Did I not tell you that if you believed, you would see the glory of God?” He lifts his eyes and thanks the Father, and “he cried with a loud voice, ‘Lazarus, come out!’ The dead man came out, his hands and feet bound with strips of cloth.” St Leo the Great wrote that it belongs to the man in Christ to weep over a dead friend, and to the God in Christ to call him back to life by a word (in substance). One Person, true God and true man, weeps and raises. And the last command is given to the bystanders: “Unbind him, and let him go.” St Augustine saw here an image of the sinner who comes out of the tomb of sin by confessing: Christ alone gives life, but he has entrusted to his Church the ministry of unbinding (in substance). Before Easter, there is no better way to keep Lazarus Saturday than to come out of our tomb in the sacrament of Confession and let the Church unbind us.

Lazarus would die again; his raising was a sign. Paul proclaims the reality it points to: “But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead, the first fruits of those who have died… for as all die in Adam, so all will be made alive in Christ.” Christ's Resurrection is not a return to this life but the first fruits of the harvest of the risen body, and “the last enemy to be destroyed is death.” Genesis today closes the story of Rebekah. Her family asks her one question: “Will you go with this man?” and she answers in one word: “I will.” She leaves her home for a bridegroom she has never seen. St Ambrose saw in Rebekah the Church, and every soul, going out in faith to meet Christ (in substance). Abraham's servant says, “Do not delay me.” Tomorrow the Lord rides into Jerusalem. Will we go with this man? With Rebekah, let us answer, “I will.”
outline: Opening
Ask: have you ever stood at the grave of someone you loved?
Point 1 · Jesus began to weep
True man, he shares our grief.
Point 2 · Lazarus, come out! Unbind him
True God, he gives life; the Church unbinds.
Point 3 · The first fruits
Christ's Resurrection and ours; death the last enemy.
Point 4 · Will you go with this man?
Rebekah's “I will” on the eve of Hosanna.
Take-home line
“If you believed, you would see the glory of God.”
live: Come out and be unbound (John 11:44)
Make a good Confession before Easter; if you have been away a long time, go this coming week.
Weep with those who weep (John 11:35)
Visit or call a family who has lost someone this year, and pray with them for the dead.
Say I will (Genesis 24:58)
Tomorrow, carrying your palm, tell the Lord in your own words that you will go with him through this Holy Week.
2027-03-20.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you wept at the tomb of your friend Lazarus and called him out by your word. You are true man, who shares our grief, and true God, who gives life to the dead. Call us out of every tomb of sin and fear, and let your Church unbind us in the sacrament of mercy. Strengthen our faith in the resurrection of the body, for you are the first fruits of those who have died. And as we come to Hosanna Sunday, give us Rebekah's ready answer, that we may say, “I will,” and go with you into Jerusalem, to your Cross and your Resurrection. Amen.
altar: The Lord who called Lazarus from the tomb gives us at the altar his own risen Body, the pledge of our resurrection.

2027-03-22.title: Hasha Monday · Monday of Passion Week
readings: The Lord a garland of glory; “This is rest; give rest to the weary”
They will perish, but you remain
By what authority are you doing these things?
2027-03-22.alt: Hasha Week, the week of the Lord's Passion (Kashtanubhava Azhcha), which began on the evening of Hosanna Sunday. The Panchangam notes that the newly prepared Hasha Week lectionary gives an Old Testament reading, an Epistle and a Gospel for every hour of prayer this week; the readings below are the ones the Panchangam lists for the day. The Panchangam also remembers Rev. Fr Seraphion Attupurathu OIC (Alexander Shemmashan), who came into Catholic communion in the reunion of 1930 and died in 1975.
2027-03-22.verse: But you are the same, and your years will never end.
theo: Last evening, as Hosanna Sunday closed, our Church entered Hasha Week. Hasho is the Syriac word for suffering: this is the week of the Lord's Passion, and the Church walks beside him day by day. On Monday the Gospel finds Jesus in the temple at Jerusalem, teaching, a few days before his death. The chief priests and the elders come with a question: “By what authority are you doing these things, and who gave you this authority?” Jesus answers with a question of his own: “Did the baptism of John come from heaven, or was it of human origin?” They weigh the answer by what it will cost them, not by what is true, and at last say: “We do not know.” St John Chrysostom notes that the Lord did not refuse to answer people who wished to learn, but people who asked only in order to trap him (in substance). The question is not only theirs. Each of us knows how to say “We do not know” when the truth would ask too much. This week Jesus will answer the question of his authority, not with argument, but with the Cross and the empty tomb.

Isaiah shows why some do not hear. God offers himself as “a garland of glory, and a diadem of beauty, to the remnant of his people,” but the leaders of the city are drunk: “the priest and the prophet reel with strong drink.” They mock the prophet's plain teaching as baby talk, “precept upon precept... line upon line, here a little, there a little.” Yet the message God sent was simple and kind: “This is rest; give rest to the weary; and this is repose”; “yet they would not hear.” The Letter to the Hebrews then lifts our eyes to who it is that stands in the temple. To the Son the Father says: “In the beginning, Lord, you founded the earth, and the heavens are the work of your hands; they will perish, but you remain.” Everything wears out like clothing, “But you are the same, and your years will never end.” The man questioned in the temple courts is the Lord who laid the foundations of the earth. He has every authority, and he uses it this week to lay down his life for us.

How does a family keep Hasha Week? First, by going with the Church to the prayers of the hours. This week our Church prays the Evening, Compline, Night, Morning, Third, Sixth and Ninth Hours with special solemnity, and the new Hasha Week lectionary gives readings from the Old Testament, the Apostle and the Gospel for each hour; follow your parish timetable for the hours and for the Holy Qurbono. Second, by keeping the fast and the abstinence of the Great Lent to its end, with the prostrations (kumbideel) as your parish practises them; the Panchangam asks priests to remind the faithful of the special prayers and abstinences of this week. Third, by preparing for Pesaha with a good confession before Thursday. At home, light the lamp in the evening, read the day's Gospel aloud, pray the evening prayer from the Shehimo, and end with a few moments of silence before the cross. Today we also remember Fr Seraphion Attupurathu OIC, known as Alexander Shemmashan, who came into Catholic communion in the reunion of 1930 and served the Church until his death in 1975.
outline: Opening
Ask: when have I said “I do not know” because the truth would cost me?
Point 1 · By what authority?
The question in the temple and the answer of the Cross.
Point 2 · This is rest
God's simple word, and the hearts that would not hear.
Point 3 · You remain
The Lord who founded the earth goes to his Passion.
Take-home line
“But you are the same, and your years will never end.”
live: Give rest to the weary (Isaiah 28:12)
This Hasha Week, take one burden off someone tired: a chore, an errand, a visit, a meal.
Answer honestly (Matthew 21:27)
Name one truth you have been avoiding with “I do not know,” and bring it to confession before Pesaha.
2027-03-22.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, in the beginning you founded the earth, and the heavens are the work of your hands; you remain when all things wear out. In these holy days you walked into Jerusalem to suffer for us. Give us hearts that hear your word and do not evade it. Make us a people who give rest to the weary. Keep us close to you through this week of your Passion, that we may rejoice in your Resurrection. Grant eternal rest to Fr Seraphion and to all who have served your Church faithfully. Amen.
altar: The Son who will never change offers himself in the Holy Qurbono as the true rest of the weary, the living bread that does not wear out.

2027-03-23.title: Hasha Tuesday · Tuesday of Passion Week
readings: Moses, near death, commissions Joshua: “I will be with you”
The promise of entering his rest is still open
“And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself”
2027-03-23.alt: Hasha Week, the week of the Lord's Passion (Kashtanubhava Azhcha), which began on the evening of Hosanna Sunday. The Panchangam notes that the newly prepared Hasha Week lectionary gives an Old Testament reading, an Epistle and a Gospel for every hour of prayer this week; the readings below are the ones the Panchangam lists for the day.
2027-03-23.verse: And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.
theo: On Tuesday of Hasha Week the Church lets us hear the heart of Jesus as his hour comes near. Some Greeks have asked to see him, and he has spoken of the grain of wheat that must die to bear fruit. Then he says openly: “Now my soul is troubled.” He does not hide his fear from us. He is truly man, and he feels what we feel before suffering. But he does not run: “No, it is for this reason that I have come to this hour. Father, glorify your name.” A voice answers from heaven: “I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again.” St Augustine says that the Lord allowed his soul to be troubled so that the weak members of his body, when they are troubled, would not despair, but would find their own fear already carried by their Head (in substance). Then Jesus speaks of his Cross as a lifting up: “And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.” John adds: “He said this to indicate the kind of death he was to die.” The Cross is not only where he suffers; it is where he draws the whole world to himself.

The Old Testament reading takes us to the last days of Moses. “The Lord said to Moses, ‘Your time to die is near; call Joshua and present yourselves in the tent of meeting, so that I may commission him.’” Moses knows the people will be unfaithful after his death, so he writes a song to be a witness and lays the book of the law beside the ark. Then the Lord says to Joshua: “Be strong and bold, for you shall bring the Israelites into the land that I promised them; I will be with you.” Joshua's name in Hebrew is the same as the name of Jesus: “the Lord saves.” The Letter to the Hebrews draws the line from one to the other. Joshua led the people into the land, but not into God's final rest, for “if Joshua had given them rest, God would not speak later about another day.” That rest is still offered: “while the promise of entering his rest is still open, let us take care that none of you should seem to have failed to reach it... For we who have believed enter that rest.” Moses died outside the land. Jesus, the true Joshua, will die and rise, and lead us through death into the rest of God.

Jesus also says today: “The light is with you for a little longer. Walk while you have the light.” These are the days to walk in that light. Many families use Tuesday and Wednesday of Hasha Week to prepare for the great three days. The Church's own preparation is simple: finish your confession; make peace with anyone you have quarrelled with, since no one should come to the table of Pesaha with a grudge; and plan to be present for the services. On Thursday our Church celebrates Pesaha with the Holy Qurbono of the Lord's Supper and the washing of the feet. On Friday comes the long service of the Passion, with the readings of the hours, the procession and the veneration of the Cross. Saturday is the day of the Lord's rest in the tomb, and the night leads into Qyomtho, the Resurrection. At home, children can help prepare the house for Pesaha, and the family can read aloud tonight the words of Jesus about the grain of wheat (John 12:24).
outline: Opening
Ask: what do I do when I am afraid of what is coming?
Point 1 · Moses hands on the journey
“Be strong and bold... I will be with you.”
Point 2 · “Now my soul is troubled”
The fear of Jesus and his obedience.
Point 3 · Lifted up to draw all
The Cross that leads us into God's rest.
Take-home line
“And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.”
live: Make peace before Pesaha (Matthew 5:24)
Before Thursday, speak or write to one person with whom you have a quarrel, and offer peace.
Walk while you have the light (John 12:35)
Tonight switch off the screens for one hour and spend part of it reading John 12 together.
2027-03-23.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, true Joshua, you lead your people through death into the rest of God. In your hour your soul was troubled, and yet you said: Father, glorify your name. When we are afraid, let us find our fear already carried by you. Lifted up on the Cross, draw us and all people to yourself. Keep us walking in your light in these holy days, and bring us to the joy of your Resurrection. Amen.
altar: On the altar the Lord who was lifted up draws us to himself; in the Holy Qurbono we already taste the rest that is still open to us.

2027-03-24.title: Hasha Wednesday · Wednesday of Passion Week
readings: A sword drawn for slaughter: “Return it to its sheath!”
Christ offered once for all to remove sin by the sacrifice of himself
Judas: “What will you give me if I betray him to you?”
2027-03-24.alt: Hasha Week, the week of the Lord's Passion (Kashtanubhava Azhcha), which began on the evening of Hosanna Sunday. The Panchangam notes that the newly prepared Hasha Week lectionary gives an Old Testament reading, an Epistle and a Gospel for every hour of prayer this week; the readings below are the ones the Panchangam lists for the day. Tomorrow is Pesaha; in 2027 it is also the date of the Annunciation (25 March), for which the Panchangam gives readings as well: follow the direction of your eparchy.
2027-03-24.verse: But as it is, he has appeared once for all at the end of the age to remove sin by the sacrifice of himself.
theo: Hasha Wednesday brings us to one of the saddest sentences in the Gospel: “Then one of the twelve, who was called Judas Iscariot, went to the chief priests and said, ‘What will you give me if I betray him to you?’ They paid him thirty pieces of silver. And from that moment he began to look for an opportunity to betray him.” From very early times Christians kept Wednesday as a day of fasting, and ancient Church orders explain it as the day on which the betrayal was agreed (in substance). Notice that the betrayer is “one of the twelve,” a friend who had eaten with Jesus, heard him and been sent by him. The danger to the Lord came from within his own circle; the danger to our faith comes most often from within our own hearts. Thirty shekels was the price set in the Law for a slave (Exodus 21:32), and Zechariah had spoken of a shepherd valued at “thirty shekels of silver.” Our Lord lets himself be priced like a slave so that slaves may be set free. The Church teaches that the Passion cannot be blamed on any people as a whole: all sinners were the authors of his suffering, and we too (Catechism 597–598). The question for us is not only what Judas did, but what price I set on Jesus when he costs me something.

Ezekiel's oracle sounds like the clash of iron: “A sword, a sword! Drawn for slaughter, polished to consume, to flash like lightning.” It is a word of judgment on the Ammonites and on everyone who lives by false visions and lies. Just before it the prophet says that the crown will be removed “until he comes whose right it is; to him I will give it,” and Christian readers have long heard in this the coming of Christ, the true King. Then comes the strange command: “Return it to its sheath!” In the garden, a few hours after Judas has made his bargain, Jesus will say to Peter: “Put your sword back into its sheath. Am I not to drink the cup that the Father has given me?” The sword of judgment does not fall on us; the Son takes the cup instead. The Letter to the Hebrews explains what he does with that cup. Christ “entered into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God on our behalf.” He does not offer himself again and again like the high priest year by year: “he has appeared once for all at the end of the age to remove sin by the sacrifice of himself,” and “will appear a second time, not to deal with sin, but to save those who are eagerly waiting for him.” In every Holy Qurbono this one sacrifice is made present on the altar; it is not repeated, but it is truly offered for us (Catechism 1366–1367).

Tonight is the eve of Pesaha, and it helps a family to know what tomorrow holds. In the Holy Qurbono of Pesaha the Church remembers the night on which the Lord gave us his Body and Blood and instituted the priesthood. In the service of the washing of the feet the celebrant, kneeling, washes the feet of men chosen from the parish, as Jesus washed the feet of his disciples; follow the time your parish announces. At home, many St Thomas Christian families keep the Pesaha meal on Thursday night: the head of the family breaks the unleavened Pesaha bread, shares it with everyone in order of age, and the family prays together and reads the account of the Last Supper. Today, then, finish what remains: go to confession if you have not yet done so, keep the fast, help prepare the house and the Pesaha bread, and in the evening pray for Judas's opposite: a heart that, when it falls, runs back to Jesus as Peter did, and not away from him. In 2027 the Annunciation (25 March) falls on Pesaha; the Panchangam gives its readings too, so listen to how your eparchy keeps it.
outline: Opening
Ask: what price do I set on Jesus when he costs me something?
Point 1 · “Return it to its sheath”
The sword of judgment, and the Son who drinks the cup.
Point 2 · “What will you give me?”
One of the twelve, and the price of a slave.
Point 3 · Once for all
The one sacrifice made present in the Holy Qurbono.
Take-home line
“He has appeared once for all at the end of the age to remove sin by the sacrifice of himself.”
live: Do not sell him cheaply (Matthew 26:15)
Name one thing for which you are tempted to put Jesus second this week (money, approval, comfort) and choose him in that place today.
Put the sword away (Ezekiel 21:30)
Before Pesaha, lay down one harsh word or grudge you have been holding ready to use.
2027-03-24.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you let yourself be priced like a slave so that we might be set free. You put away the sword of judgment and drank the cup the Father gave you. Keep us from ever selling you for anything this world can pay. When we fall, give us the tears of Peter and not the despair of Judas. Through your one sacrifice, made present on our altar, remove our sins and prepare us to keep your Pesaha with pure hearts. Amen.
altar: The sacrifice offered once for all on the Cross is the very sacrifice made present on our altar; in the Holy Qurbono Christ appears in the presence of God on our behalf.

2027-03-29.title: Monday of Hevoro week · Easter Monday
readings: You have died to the law through the body of Christ, so that you may belong to him who has been raised
The guards are paid to say the body was stolen
2027-03-29.alt: Hevoro week, the first week of the season of Qyomtho (the Resurrection). Hevoro means white: the week is kept as one great day of Easter joy. The fast is over: the whole week is kept as Easter.
2027-03-29.verse: In the same way, my friends, you have died to the law through the body of Christ, so that you may belong to another, to him who has been raised from the dead in order that we may bear fruit for God.
theo: Christ is risen! The Church keeps this whole week as one great day of Easter, and on its first weekday she reads what happened in Jerusalem while the women were running to tell the disciples. Two reports leave the same empty tomb. The women carry the truth to the disciples; some of the guard carry it to the chief priests. And there the truth is buried under money: the soldiers are given “a large sum of money” and told, “You must say, ‘His disciples came by night and stole him away while we were asleep.’” St Augustine asked, with a smile, what kind of witnesses these were: if they were asleep, how did they see who took the body? (in substance). Matthew adds that “this story is still told among the Jews to this day,” speaking of an account that circulated in his own time, not passing judgment on a people. The first witnesses of the risen Lord, Mary Magdalene, Peter, John and the apostles, were themselves Jews, and the Church, following the Second Vatican Council (Nostra Aetate 4), never blames the Jewish people for the death of Christ. What the passage shows is something every age knows: the truth of the Resurrection can be paid to be silent, but it cannot be paid to stay dead. The tomb was empty because the very body that was crucified had been raised, glorious and alive (Catechism 640, 645).

St Paul explains what the Resurrection does to us. He uses a picture from marriage: a wife is bound to her husband as long as he lives, but if he dies she is free to belong to another. “In the same way, my friends, you have died to the law through the body of Christ, so that you may belong to another, to him who has been raised from the dead in order that we may bear fruit for God.” In Baptism we died with Christ; now we belong to the risen Lord as a bride belongs to her husband. The old life of “sinful passions” bore “fruit for death”; the new life bears fruit for God. “But now we are discharged from the law, dead to that which held us captive, so that we are slaves not under the old written code but in the new life of the Spirit.” Easter is not only a fact about Jesus. It is a new belonging for us: we are his, and he is alive.

How do we keep Hevoro week? Hevoro means white. In the early Church those baptized at Easter wore their white garments through this whole week, and the Church still treats the eight days from Qyomtho to New Sunday as one feast. On Easter night our Church proclaimed the Resurrection and shared the peace of the risen Lord with all the people; this week that joy is carried into ordinary days. Go to the Holy Qurbono on as many days as you can. Greet one another with the Easter greeting: “Christ is risen!” “He is risen indeed!” At home, light the lamp in the evening and sing or say an Easter hymn instead of the Lenten prayers; let the children tell what they saw in church at Easter. Visit or call the sick and the elderly who could not come to the Easter services, and share Easter food with someone who has little. Next Sunday is New Sunday, when the Church hears of the Lord's appearance to Thomas.
outline: Opening
Ask: who told me that Jesus is risen, and whom have I told?
Point 1 · The story money bought
Sleeping witnesses and an empty tomb.
Point 2 · Dead to the law, alive to him
A new belonging to the risen Lord.
Point 3 · Fruit for God
The new life of the Spirit.
Take-home line
“So that you may belong to another, to him who has been raised from the dead.”
live: Tell the truth of Easter (Matthew 28:15)
Greet at least three people this week with “Christ is risen!” and tell one of them why it matters to you.
Bear fruit for God (Romans 7:4)
Choose one good habit begun in Lent and keep it through the Easter season.
2027-03-29.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you are risen from the dead, and no money or lie could keep your tomb closed. Through your Body given for us we have died to the old life, so that we may belong to you. Make our lives bear fruit for God in the new life of the Spirit. Give us courage to tell the truth of your Resurrection, and gladden all who are sad this Easter with the light of your rising. You live and reign for ever. Amen.
altar: The risen body of the Lord, once laid in the tomb, is truly given to us in the Holy Qurbono, so that we may belong to him and bear fruit for God.

2027-03-30.title: Tuesday of Hevoro week · Easter Tuesday
readings: Christ our paschal lamb has been sacrificed; let us celebrate the festival
A lamp is put on the lampstand; the measure you give
2027-03-30.alt: Hevoro week, the first week of the season of Qyomtho (the Resurrection). Hevoro means white: the week is kept as one great day of Easter joy.
2027-03-30.verse: For our paschal lamb, Christ, has been sacrificed.
theo: Three days ago the Church kept Pesaha; today St Paul tells us what Pesaha now means. “For our paschal lamb, Christ, has been sacrificed. Therefore, let us celebrate the festival, not with the old yeast, the yeast of malice and evil, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.” Paul is writing to Corinth about a scandal the community had tolerated, and he uses the image every Jewish family knew: before Passover the house is searched and every bit of leaven is cleared out, because “a little yeast leavens the whole batch of dough.” The Passover lamb was sacrificed so that Israel might pass from slavery to freedom; Christ, the true Lamb, was sacrificed on the Cross so that we might pass from death to life. St John Chrysostom, commenting on these verses, said that for the Christian the whole of life is a festival, because the Lamb has been offered for us (in substance). We keep that festival above all at the altar, where the Lamb who was sacrificed and is now risen gives himself to us, truly present, Body and Blood, soul and divinity. Many St Thomas Christian homes ate unleavened Pesaha bread last Thursday; Paul asks us to become unleavened bread ourselves, people of sincerity and truth.

The Gospel continues the Easter light. “Is a lamp brought in to be put under the bushel basket, or under the bed, and not on the lampstand? For there is nothing hidden, except to be disclosed; nor is anything secret, except to come to light.” On Good Friday the light of the world was hidden in the tomb; on Qyomtho it was set on the lampstand for all to see. No stone could keep it under the bed. Now the risen Lord puts his light in us, and he does not want it hidden by fear or by shame. Then Jesus adds a warning that is also a promise: “Pay attention to what you hear; the measure you give will be the measure you get, and still more will be given you.” Easter faith grows when it is given away. The one who shares the joy of the Resurrection receives more of it; the one who keeps it under the bed may find even what he has slipping away.

Hevoro week is a good time to clear out old yeast. Paul names it: malice and evil. In a family it may be an old resentment, a habit of sarcasm, a lie that has never been put right. Easter is the moment to throw it out, as a household clears the leaven before the feast. Practically: go to the Holy Qurbono today if you can, and receive the Lamb with a clean heart; this evening, let each person at home say one thing he or she is sorry for and one thing he or she is thankful for; and then set your Easter light on the lampstand by one visible act of goodness tomorrow, at work, in school or in the neighbourhood. Keep greeting one another with the Easter greeting all this week.
outline: Opening
Ask: what old yeast is still in my house this Easter?
Point 1 · Our paschal lamb
Christ sacrificed, the Lamb we receive.
Point 2 · Clean out the old yeast
Sincerity and truth instead of malice.
Point 3 · The lamp on the lampstand
Easter light that grows when it is shared.
Take-home line
“For our paschal lamb, Christ, has been sacrificed.”
live: Clear out the old yeast (1 Corinthians 5:7)
Name one resentment or habit of malice and give it up this week as your Easter offering.
Put the lamp on the lampstand (Mark 4:21)
Do one visible act of goodness tomorrow, without hiding that you do it because Christ is risen.
2027-03-30.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, our paschal Lamb, you were sacrificed for us and you are risen. Clear out of our hearts the old yeast of malice and evil, and make us unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. You give yourself to us at your altar; make our whole life a festival of thanksgiving. Let the light you have kindled in us shine on the lampstand, so that others may see it and come to you. Amen.
altar: On the altar the paschal Lamb, sacrificed once and now risen, gives himself to us truly; this is the festival Paul calls us to keep.

2027-03-31.title: Wednesday of Hevoro week · Easter Wednesday
readings: Fight the good fight, having faith and a good conscience
“For mortals it is impossible, but not for God”
2027-03-31.alt: Hevoro week, the first week of the season of Qyomtho (the Resurrection). Hevoro means white: the week is kept as one great day of Easter joy. The Panchangam prints the Gospel as “Mark 10:1-7–27”; it is read here as Mark 10:17–27 (the rich man), taking the first hyphen as a typesetting break. Please verify locally.
2027-03-31.verse: For mortals it is impossible, but not for God; for God all things are possible.
theo: On this Easter Wednesday the Gospel tells of a man who “ran up and knelt before” Jesus and asked: “Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?” He has kept the commandments since his youth, and Mark adds one of the tenderest lines in the Gospels: “Jesus, looking at him, loved him.” Out of that love comes the call: “You lack one thing; go, sell what you own, and give the money to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me.” But “he was shocked and went away grieving, for he had many possessions.” Clement of Alexandria, in his little book on this passage, taught that what the Lord asks us to leave is above all the grip of wealth on the soul, the passions that make us its slaves, so that riches become a servant of love and not a master (in substance). The disciples are astonished: “Then who can be saved?” And Jesus answers: “For mortals it is impossible, but not for God; for God all things are possible.” In Easter week this sentence shines with new light. Four days ago the most impossible thing of all happened: a man who had died on a cross and been laid in a tomb rose bodily from the dead. The God who did that can also loosen the grip of possessions on a human heart.

St Paul's charge to Timothy fits the same road: “I am giving you these instructions, Timothy, my child... so that by following them you may fight the good fight, having faith and a good conscience.” Faith and conscience go together like the two oars of a boat. “By rejecting conscience, certain persons have suffered shipwreck in the faith; among them are Hymenaeus and Alexander.” Paul's severe discipline, handing them over “to Satan,” has a healing purpose: “so that they may learn not to blaspheme.” The Church corrects in order to bring back, never simply to cast out. The Second Vatican Council calls conscience the most secret core and sanctuary of a person, where one is alone with God (Gaudium et Spes 16). The rich man's conscience told him the truth when Jesus spoke; his possessions told him to walk away. Easter gives us the strength to listen to the first voice. The risen Lord, who says “Peace be with you” to his frightened disciples, also gives us his Spirit to keep our consciences clear and our faith afloat.

Hevoro week continues: keep it as Easter. Go to the Holy Qurbono if you can, and keep using the Easter greeting. This week is also a good moment to make an Easter gift of what you have, as the rich man was invited to do: give something you value to someone poor, not only something you would have thrown away. Each night before sleeping, a family can make a short examination of conscience together: where did we follow Jesus today, and where did we walk away? Then entrust everything to the God for whom all things are possible. On Sunday, New Sunday, the Church will hear how the risen Lord came through closed doors to Thomas; prepare to meet him there with your own questions.
outline: Opening
Ask: what possession would I find hardest to give up for Jesus?
Point 1 · Fight the good fight
Faith and a good conscience, the two oars.
Point 2 · Jesus, looking at him, loved him
The call that comes from love.
Point 3 · For God all things are possible
The impossible of Easter, and of our hearts.
Take-home line
“For God all things are possible.”
live: Treasure in heaven (Mark 10:21)
This Easter week, give something you value to someone who is poor.
Keep a good conscience (1 Timothy 1:19)
Each night this week, take two minutes as a family to ask: where did we follow Jesus today, and where did we walk away?
2027-03-31.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you looked on the rich man and loved him, and you look on us with the same love. Loosen the grip of our possessions on our hearts, and give us courage to follow you. Keep our consciences clear and our faith whole, so that we may fight the good fight to the end. You rose from the dead, for whom all things are possible: do in us what we cannot do alone. You live and reign for ever. Amen.
altar: At the altar the Lord who gave everything, even his own Body and Blood, gives himself to us: the true treasure in heaven, already given on earth.

quick: Jesus sees the bent woman and sets her free.
God's sabbath rest is our freedom and healing.
Healed ourselves, we become Good Samaritans.
2027-03-07.action: Stop for one person in need you would usually pass by.
2027-03-07.question: What has bent me down, and do I let Jesus lift me up?
2027-03-07.special: K'piphtho Sunday, fifth Sunday of the Great Fast.
illus: An illustration

An old woman in a Kerala village had walked bent for years with a back problem. After an operation she stood straight and said with tears: “I can see the sky again.” Sin and sorrow can bend the soul in the same way.

family.explain: A woman could not stand up straight for eighteen years. Jesus touched her, and she stood up straight and praised God!
family.intention: We pray for people who carry heavy burdens and for all who are sick.
family.ask: Ask: “Whom can we help this week, like the Good Samaritan?”

catechism: The sabbath and works of mercy.
kidsaint: The Forty Martyrs of Sebaste (9 Mar)

Forty Christian soldiers in Armenia who were made to stand on a frozen lake because they would not give up Jesus. They encouraged one another and stayed faithful together. Lesson: help your friends stay faithful.
term: K'piphtho means “the bent (crippled) woman”. The fifth Sunday of the Great Fast reads her healing (Luke 13:10–17).
termMore: The Syriac and Greek Fathers read the parable as the story of salvation: humanity wounded on the road, Christ the Samaritan, the oil and wine of the sacraments, the inn of the Church.

quick: Jesus is the light of the world: he opens blind eyes.
Faith grows step by step: “Lord, I believe.”
Bartimaeus receives sight and follows Jesus on the way.
2027-03-14.action: Pray often this week: “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me.”
2027-03-14.question: Where am I still blind, and do I want to see?
2027-03-14.special: Samio Sunday, sixth Sunday of the Great Fast. Announce the Fortieth Friday (19 Mar), Lazarus Saturday (20 Mar) and Hosanna Sunday (21 Mar); remind the faithful to bring palm leaves and flowers.
illus: An illustration

Free eye camps in Kerala villages give sight to hundreds every year. One old man, after his cataract operation, said: “Now I can see my grandchildren's faces.” Jesus came to give us a sight even greater: to see God's face in Christ.

family.explain: A blind man called Bartimaeus shouted to Jesus for help. Jesus asked what he wanted, and he said: “I want to see!” Jesus healed him, and he followed Jesus.
family.intention: We pray for the blind and for those who have lost faith.
family.ask: Ask: “How will our family keep Holy Week this year?”

kidsaint: The husband of Mary and the foster father of Jesus, a carpenter who worked hard, protected his family and obeyed God at once. Lesson: work well and take care of your family.
term: Samio is Syriac for “the blind man”. The sixth Sunday of the Great Fast, the last before Hosanna Sunday, reads the healing of the blind.
termMore: The Fortieth Friday and Lazarus Saturday

On the Friday before Hosanna Sunday the forty days of the Fast are completed (the lectionary notes no fasting or prostrations that day). The next day remembers the raising of Lazarus, and Holy Week follows.

quick: Hosanna: the humble King enters Jerusalem on a donkey.
If we are silent, the stones will shout.
Hosanna means “Save us”: enter Holy Week with Christ.
2027-03-21.action: Take part in every service of Holy Week this year.
2027-03-21.question: Will my Hosanna today still be faithful on Friday?
2027-03-21.special: Hosanna (Palm) Sunday: blessing of palms and procession. Holy Week begins this evening; remind the faithful about the special prayers and abstinence. (In 2025–26 also Social Welfare Day; check the collection.)
illus: An illustration

In Kerala, children carry the blessed tender palm leaves home and their grandmothers weave them into small crosses for the door. The palm that welcomed the King becomes the sign of his Cross. That is Holy Week in one leaf.

family.explain: Jesus rode into Jerusalem on a little donkey. People waved palm branches and shouted “Hosanna!” They welcomed him as their King.
family.intention: We pray that our family may keep Holy Week well and welcome Jesus as King.
family.ask: Ask: “Which services of Holy Week will we attend together?”

kidsaint: When Jesus entered the city, children in the Temple kept shouting “Hosanna to the Son of David!” Jesus said that God had prepared praise from the mouths of children (Matthew 21:15–16). Lesson: your praise matters to Jesus.
term: Hosanna is Hebrew for “Save us, we pray”. On the Sunday before Easter the Church blesses palms and celebrates the Lord's entry into Jerusalem; Holy Week (Hasho) begins in the evening.
termMore: The palms are kept at home through the year; in the Malankara tradition they may be brought back and used in the fire of the Yaldo night service, so that the same palms that welcomed the King greet his birth.

quick: On this night Jesus gave us the Holy Qurbono.
He is the true Passover Lamb who saves us.
The One who gives his Body washes our feet: Eucharist and service.
2027-03-25.action: Spend time in adoration tonight, keeping Jesus company.
2027-03-25.question: How do I prepare to receive the Lord's Body and Blood?
2027-03-25.special: Pesaha (Maundy Thursday): Holy Qurbono of the Lord's Supper and the washing of the feet. In 2027 also the date of the Annunciation; follow the eparchy's direction.
illus: An illustration

On Pesaha night St Thomas Christian families gather around the table, and the eldest breaks the Pesaha appam marked with a cross and shares it with everyone, even those away abroad who are remembered by name. The whole family becomes an upper room.

family.explain: On the night before he died, Jesus had a special meal with his friends. He took bread and said, “This is my body,” and the cup, “This is my blood.” That is how he gave us Holy Qurbana.
family.intention: We thank God for the Holy Qurbono and pray for our priests.
family.ask: Ask: “What can each of us do to serve someone in our family this week?”

kidsaint: The youngest apostle, who rested his head on Jesus' chest at the Last Supper and later stood at the foot of the Cross with Mary. Lesson: stay close to Jesus, especially when it is hard.
term: From the Hebrew for “Passover”. Maundy Thursday, when the Lord instituted the Holy Qurbono and washed the disciples' feet. Kerala Christian families break the Pesaha appam at home in the evening.
termMore: At the Pesaha service the bishop or priest washes the feet of twelve persons, as Jesus did (John 13:1–15), showing that the Eucharist leads to humble service.

quick: “He was wounded for our transgressions.”
From the Cross: forgiveness, Paradise, and Mary given to us.
“It is finished”: the work of salvation is complete.
2027-03-26.action: Forgive one person today, as Jesus forgave from the Cross.
2027-03-26.question: What does the Cross ask of me today?
2027-03-26.special: Good Friday: day of fasting; no Holy Qurbono; veneration of the Cross. Collection for the Holy Land.
illus: An illustration

In many Kerala homes on Good Friday the television is switched off, the family eats only kanji, and an old crucifix is placed on the table. The children ask why. A grandmother answers: “Because today Jesus died for you.”

family.explain: Jesus died on the cross because he loves us. Even on the cross he forgave the people who hurt him, and he promised heaven to the thief who asked for mercy.
family.intention: We pray for all who are suffering, and we thank Jesus for his love.
family.ask: Ask: “Is there someone I need to forgive today?”

catechism: Mary at the foot of the Cross.
kidsaint: One of the men crucified beside Jesus said: “Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom.” Jesus promised: “Today you will be with me in Paradise.” (Later tradition calls him Dismas.) Lesson: it is never too late to turn to Jesus.
term: The day of the Lord's Passion and death. In the Malankara tradition the long service of the Hours is prayed, the Cross is venerated and then laid to rest, recalling the burial of the Lord, and the faithful keep fast.
termMore: Because on this day, through the suffering of Christ, the greatest good was done: the redemption of the world. In Malayalam it is called the Friday of sorrow; both names are true.

quick: Holy Saturday: the great silence; the Lord rests in the tomb.
He descended to the dead to free Adam and the just of old.
Buried with him in Baptism, we wait to rise with him.
2027-03-27.action: Spend part of today in silent prayer.
2027-03-27.question: What in me must be buried, so that I can rise with Christ?
2027-03-27.special: Holy Saturday: the Church waits at the tomb; preparation for the night of the Resurrection.
illus: An illustration
On Holy Saturday Kerala homes are quiet: the kitchen prepares the Easter meal, but no one plays loud music. Children are told: “Jesus is in the tomb; tonight he will rise.” The whole house waits.

family.explain: After Jesus died, his friends laid him in a tomb and rolled a big stone in front. His enemies sealed it and put guards there. But they could not stop what God was going to do!
family.intention: We pray for people who are sad and have lost hope.
family.ask: Ask: “How can we get ready for Easter together?”

kidsaint: A rich and respected man who was a secret disciple of Jesus. After Jesus died, he bravely asked Pilate for his body and laid him in his own new tomb. Lesson: be brave to show your love for Jesus.
term: The day between the Cross and the Resurrection, when Christ rests in the tomb and descends to the dead. It is kept in silence and prayer; the celebration of Qyomtho begins in the night.
termMore: An article of the Creed: after his death Christ went to the realm of the dead (Sheol) not to suffer but to free the righteous who had gone before him (1 Peter 3:18–19; 4:6).

quick: Christ is risen: “He is not here; he has been raised.”
The empty tomb and the meeting with the risen Lord give birth to faith.
Because Christ is risen, death is defeated: live as Easter people.
2027-03-28.action: Greet everyone with “Christ is risen!” throughout this week.
2027-03-28.question: What difference does the Resurrection make to my life this week?
2027-03-28.special: Qyomtho, the Resurrection of our Lord: day of obligation; Holy Qurbono for the people. Hevoro week follows.
illus: An illustration

On Easter night in Kerala the church bells ring after weeks of silence, the people light candles from the paschal flame, and the dark church fills with light. A child once asked: “Did Jesus switch on the lights?” In a way, yes: he lit up the world.

family.explain: On Easter morning the women went to Jesus' tomb, but it was empty! An angel said: “He is risen!” Then Jesus himself met them. Jesus is alive for ever!
family.intention: We thank God for Easter joy and pray for all who are sad or sick.
family.ask: Ask: “How can we share Easter joy with someone this week?”

kidsaint: She stayed at the Cross and came first to the tomb on Easter morning. The risen Jesus called her by name and sent her to tell the apostles. Lesson: tell others that Jesus is alive!
term: Syriac for “resurrection”. The feast of feasts, the Resurrection of our Lord, and the season of fifty days that follows until Pentecost.
termMore: The week after Easter, called Hevoro (white) week, recalling the white garments of the newly baptised and the joy of the Resurrection.

quick: Abraham, who wronged Abimelech out of fear, prayed for him, and God healed his house.
Paul prays that the Lord of peace will give peace at all times and in all ways.
Jesus walks on the sea, calls Peter, and catches him when he begins to sink.
2027-03-01.action: Pray today for someone you have wronged or misjudged.
2027-03-01.question: Where am I looking at the wind instead of at Jesus?

family.explain: The disciples were in a boat in a big storm at night. Jesus came to them walking on the water and said: be brave, it is me, do not be afraid. Peter walked on the water too, but when he looked at the waves he got scared and started to sink. He shouted: Lord, save me! And Jesus held his hand at once.
family.intention: We pray for everyone who is afraid tonight.
family.ask: Ask: “What makes us afraid, and how can we say ‘Lord, save me’ together?”

illus: An illustration

A fisherman from Vizhinjam remembers the night his small boat lost its engine far from the shore. The swell was high and the radio was dead. His younger brother began to panic and wanted to jump and swim. The older man held him by the shirt and said: look at the lighthouse, only at the lighthouse, not at the waves. They rowed through the night with their eyes on that one turning light. At dawn a bigger boat found them. He says: the waves never stopped; I just stopped looking at them.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, you come to us in every storm. Take away our fear and give us your peace. Amen.
share: Abraham prayed to God; and God healed Abimelech (Genesis 20:17). Whom have I wronged, and have I prayed for them?
May the Lord of peace himself give you peace at all times in all ways (2 Thessalonians 3:16). Where do I most need God's peace?
Lord, save me! (Matthew 14:30). When did I last cry out to Jesus like Peter?
pm.resp: Lord, save us; give us your peace.
interc: For all who are afraid, especially the sick and those who live alone.
For fishermen and all who work at sea, especially on the coasts of Kerala.
For those we have hurt or misjudged, and for reconciliation in families.
For all who feel the Great Fast becoming heavy at its midpoint.
For peace in our country and in the world.
pm.close: Father, your Son walked on the waters and caught Peter as he sank. Give us faith to step out at his word, humility to pray for those we have wronged, and the peace that comes only from him. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

quick: God kept his promise: Sarah bore Isaac, and her laughter became joy.
In baptism we were clothed with Christ and became heirs of the promise to Abraham.
Jesus reproaches the towns that saw his miracles and did not repent.
2027-03-02.action: Find the date of your baptism and give thanks for it.
2027-03-02.question: Which of God's graces to me has not yet changed my life?

family.explain: Abraham and Sarah waited many, many years for a baby. They were very old. But God had promised, and God kept his promise: baby Isaac was born! His name means “he laughs,” because Sarah laughed with happiness. God always keeps his promises.
family.intention: We pray for couples who are waiting for a child, and for all who are waiting for God's help.
family.ask: Ask: “Do we know the day each of us was baptized? Let us find out together.”

illus: An illustration

A couple in Pathanamthitta waited eleven years for a child. Every First Friday they went to the same small chapel, and the old sacristan, who knew their story, would nod to them as they came in. When their daughter was finally born, they brought her to the chapel at two weeks old. The sacristan, now walking with a stick, looked at the baby and began to laugh, and then to cry, and then to laugh again. He said: I have been praying for this child for eleven years too. You did not know that, did you?

pm.open: Faithful Father, you keep every promise. Fill us with the joy of your children. Amen.
share: The Lord did for Sarah as he had promised (Genesis 21:1). Which promise of God am I still waiting to see fulfilled?
As many of you as were baptized into Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ (Galatians 3:27). Do I live as someone clothed with Christ?
They would have repented long ago (Matthew 11:21). What grace have I received many times without changing?
pm.resp: Lord, keep your promise in us.
interc: For couples longing for children.
For all who have lost hope after long waiting.
For the newly baptized and for parents and godparents.
For the conversion of hearts in our parish this Lent.
For unity among all the baptized, one in Christ Jesus.
pm.close: Father, you made us your children in Christ and heirs of the promise to Abraham. Let the graces we receive bear fruit in repentance, and turn our tears into the laughter of Easter. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

quick: At the middle of the Great Fast the Church lifts up the Holy Cross; the Panchangam calls it the setting up of Golgotha.
As Moses lifted up the bronze serpent, the Son of Man is lifted up, so that whoever believes in him may have eternal life.
God is faithful and will not let us be tested beyond our strength; thus far the Lord has helped us.
2027-03-03.action: Spend five minutes looking at a crucifix in silence today.
2027-03-03.question: What has the Lord helped me with in the first half of the Fast, and what do I need to take up again?
term: The middle of the Great Fast, kept on the Wednesday of the fourth week. The Holy Cross is lifted up and honoured, often set up in the middle of the church as a sign of Golgotha, to strengthen the faithful for the second half of the Fast.
kidsaint: Today is the middle of the Great Fast. The Church puts up the Cross to remind us where we are walking: to Good Friday and to Easter Sunday. Lesson: when you get tired of being good, look at the Cross and remember how much Jesus loves you.

family.explain: In the desert, snakes bit the people. God told Moses to make a bronze snake and lift it up on a pole. Anyone who looked at it was healed. Jesus said he would be lifted up on the Cross like that, so that everyone who looks at him with faith will have life with God. Today, in the middle of the Great Fast, the Church lifts up the Cross for us to look at.
family.intention: We pray that our family may keep the Fast faithfully until Easter.
